title: new_profile's plain-scroll labels have no compositor owner
description:
serviceMarquees takes LV_LABEL_LONG_SCROLL_CIRCULAR only. lv_label.c's
set_ofs_x_anim invalidates the label on every scroll tick and the label patch
does not guard it, so a plain LV_LABEL_LONG_SCROLL label that overflows
invalidates its own box at the animation rate with nothing owning it.

Four such labels are on the new_profile screen (screens.c obj33, obj36, obj38,
obj39). obj33 is LV_SIZE_CONTENT and can never overflow. The other three are
85, 85 and 250 px wide, and today's text fits, so the screen measures 0.00
invalidations a second over 40 s (tools/inval_sweep.py, bench board,
2026-09-15). A longer profile name or a wider value would start it.

Not a defect today, so this is a decision rather than a fix: either extend
serviceMarquees to the non-circular mode, or leave it and accept that the
screen's cost depends on its text. new_profile is already the most expensive
page in the build (165 ms of LVGL draw, 104k overlay pixels), so an 85 px box
scrolling is small next to what the page costs anyway.
notes: Decided 2026-10-01, owner delegated the default: leave serviceMarquees circular only. Today's text fits the three 85, 85 and 250 px boxes and the screen measures 0.00 invalidations a second, and new_profile already costs 165 ms of LVGL draw and 104k overlay pixels, so an 85 px plain scroll is small against the page. The rule stays recorded in CLAUDE.md (UI-pipeline invariants): widening those labels or a longer profile name starts the churn, and the fix then is to extend serviceMarquees to LV_LABEL_LONG_SCROLL. Closed.

title: Reading the framebuffer endpoint hard displaces bands on the panel
description:
Reading the framebuffer endpoint at a sustained rate displaces bands on the
panel. The instrument disturbs the thing it is used to inspect, and nothing
recorded that until now.

## What was seen

Bench board, 2026-09-13, `display-loadtest` at affbc12f, pixel clock divider 7,
during gm-t9ld's probe: 336 rounds over 15 minutes, one round every 2.7 s, each
round reading a whole step 1 dump of 460,800 bytes.

`GM_SCANOUT` resyncs sat at 0 for the first 250 s, climbed to 71 by 930 s, and
stopped climbing the moment the probe stopped. That is about one displaced band
per four whole reads. `slips` stayed 0 throughout.

The mechanism is not mysterious. The endpoint msyncs all 460,800 bytes out and
back and then streams them, against the bounce refill, on a bus the panel is
already reading from at 24 MB/s or more. CLAUDE.md's hardware invariants
describe exactly this class of fault: the refill falls behind, laps the eight
buffer pool, and the VSYNC square-up displaces one band.

## Why it matters, and what it does not undermine

Every visual check in this repo runs through `/api/debug/fb`. CLAUDE.md is
explicit that the framebuffer endpoint is the way to verify the panel and that
the camera is not ("the photos are too dark to classify"). So this is a
property of the main verification instrument.

**The likely reading, which this bead has to confirm rather than assume:** the
disturbance is in the scan-out and not in the dump. The endpoint reads
framebuffer memory, while a displaced band is a refill timing fault downstream
of that memory, so the bytes returned should be the bytes LVGL and the render
task wrote. If that holds, every gradient result taken through this endpoint
stands, including gm-nov3.5's 576,000 sample sweep over all 60 built-ins and
gm-nov3.22's runs, and the only cost is cosmetic and transient.

If it does not hold, the consequences are much larger and reach several closed
beads, which is why the first job here is to establish it rather than to assert
it.

## What to do

Settle the reading first. Then decide whether anything needs to change, and be
willing to conclude that nothing does: a documented cost on a debug endpoint
may be the right answer for a tool no production device is polling.

Worth weighing: a rate at which the endpoint is safe, if one exists, so a
future probe can be written to stay under it; whether the endpoint can avoid
the full msync, since the round trip is the expensive half; and whether the
scan-out counters should be reported beside a dump so a caller can see that its
own reads are costing bands.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] It is established, with evidence, whether the disturbance affects the
      bytes the endpoint returns or only what the panel scans out.
- [ ] If only the scan-out: that is written into CLAUDE.md beside the existing
      framebuffer endpoint guidance, with the measured rate and the resync
      count, and this bead records that the gradient results taken through the
      endpoint are unaffected and why.
- [ ] If the dump itself can be affected: the closed beads that relied on it
      are named, and a bead is raised for each.
- [ ] The read rate at which resyncs begin to climb is measured, rather than
      described as hard polling. State reads per second and the resync rate at
      two or more rates.
- [ ] `slips` is confirmed to stay at 0 at every rate tested, since a slip and
      a resync are different faults and only one of them was seen here.
notes:
Lead note, 2026-09-13, from reading the handler rather than the board.

Two things the handler shows that make the work here cheaper.

First, a discriminator that costs one extra sweep. The full `esp_cache_msync`
pair runs once per request, before any byte is filled, over all 460,800 bytes,
whatever `step` says (`WebUIPluginDebug.cpp:1903` to `:1910`). The streaming
after it is proportional to `step`: at step 8 the body is 1/64 of the bytes. So
the two candidate causes predict opposite things. If the msync is the cause,
bands displaced per request stay about the same from step 1 to step 8. If the
streaming is the cause, they fall by roughly 64 times. Run the same probe at
step 1 and step 8 for equal numbers of requests and read `resyncs` from
`GM_SCANOUT` for each. That names the cause without building anything, and it
also answers whether a lower resolution dump is a safe rate, which the bead asks
about.

Second, a coherence property worth stating whichever way the main question
lands, because it is separate from it. A dump is not atomic. The msync is one
shot at the start, and the body is then filled across many send rounds while the
compositor keeps writing. The picture that comes back is torn in time whenever
the buffer being read is written during the read. It does not matter for a
static picture, which is what gm-nov3.5 and gm-nov3.22 both read (a gradient
ramp that changes only when a setting changes), so neither result is threatened
by this. It does matter for anything that reads a dump of a moving picture and
treats it as one instant. Say so in whatever goes into CLAUDE.md, because it is
the kind of thing a future probe will assume the other way.

Neither of these settles the main question. The bytes still have to be shown to
be the bytes that were written. The reading above supports the expected answer:
the msync invalidates before the fill, so every byte is fetched from PSRAM after
the writeback, and a displaced band is a refill deadline missed downstream of
that memory. That is an argument, not the evidence the first criterion asks for.

Board session answer, 2026-09-13, recorded by the lead from the board lane's report so it is not lost with the message.

**The disturbance is in the scan-out only. The bytes the endpoint returns are the bytes that were written.** That is the first acceptance criterion, and every gradient result taken through this endpoint stands, including gm-nov3.5's sweep and gm-nov3.22's runs.

The argument, and then the evidence.

The endpoint writes nothing to the framebuffer. It flushes the cache (writeback, then invalidate) and streams the same PSRAM the render task wrote. A resync is the VSYNC square-up that happens when the bounce refill falls behind. That is downstream of framebuffer memory, so it changes which rows the panel shows and never what the buffer holds.

Two things in the record support it. `slips` stayed 0 for the whole window while `resyncs` climbed to 71, and a slip is the counter for a refill that actually missed its data. And the endpoint's own output stayed correct under exactly the traffic that causes the resyncs: the job four run compared 38,400 samples through `/api/debug/fb` against the expected ramp with 0 mismatches, and gm-nov3.10's earlier batch did the same over 172,800 samples. A ramp comparison of that size is where a corrupted dump would show.

**The rate, on record.** One whole step 1 read (460,800 bytes) per round, one round every 2.7 seconds: 0.37 reads a second, about 170 kB per second of framebuffer streaming. Over the 680 seconds between the first resync and the last, that is about 252 reads for 71 resyncs, so roughly **0.28 resyncs per whole step 1 read**. This is not a burst rate. **Superseded: read the later section in these notes before quoting 0.28.** It was one boot and did not reproduce. The reproducible figure for the same probe pattern is 0.041 per read, and paced reads measured zero, so 0.28 is an upper bound seen once rather than the rate.

Still open here: the step 1 against step 8 discriminator, which separates the once per request cache flush from the streaming, and would say whether a lower resolution dump is a safe rate. The flush covers all 460,800 bytes whatever `step` says, so flat means the flush is the cause and a fall of about 64 times means the streaming is.

2026-09-13, both questions answered on the board, and the original per-read
rate corrected.

Build: display-loadtest reported as v1.9.8-sleep9-672-gb24b3fcb-dirty, built
2026-09-13T14:04:01Z. Bench board, pixel clock divider 7, stored and live.
Counters read from /api/debug/scanout rather than the serial log, which is the
same source GM_SCANOUT prints from and costs one small GET per arm.

## 1. THE DUMP'S BYTES ARE NOT AFFECTED. ONLY THE SCAN-OUT IS.

The reading in the description holds, and three things support it.

The endpoint writes nothing. It msyncs (writeback, then invalidate) and then
streams the same PSRAM the render task wrote. A resync is the VSYNC square-up
when the bounce refill falls behind, which is downstream of framebuffer
memory, so it changes which rows the panel shows and never what the buffer
holds.

slips stayed 0 in every measurement below and in the original observation. A
slip is the counter for a refill that missed its data; a resync is the
recovery that follows a refill running late. Nothing reported missing data.

The endpoint's own output stayed correct under exactly the traffic that
produces the resyncs. On this board, 2026-09-13, gradient_fb_check compared
38,400 samples read through /api/debug/fb against the expected ramp with 0
mismatches, and gm-nov3.10's earlier batch did 172,800 with 0. A comparison of
that size is where a disturbed dump would show.

So every gradient result taken through this endpoint stands, gm-nov3.5's
576,000 sample sweep included. The cost is cosmetic and transient.

## 2. THE CAUSE IS THE CACHE FLUSH, NOT THE STREAMING

The endpoint flushes all 460,800 bytes once per request before any byte is
filled, whatever step says (WebUIPluginDebug.cpp, the esp_cache_msync pair),
and streams w/step by h/step pixels after it. So step 1 and step 8 pay the
same flush and 64 times different streaming.

Same round pattern, same cadence, same request count, only the step changed:

  step   rounds   bytes/read   resyncs   per read   frames   fps
     1      145      460,800         6      0.041   15,753   43.4
     8      145        7,200         4      0.028   15,753   43.4

64 times less streaming bought a factor of 1.5, and with counts of 6 and 4
that is inside Poisson noise. Flat. **The flush is the cause.**

Two consequences. A lower resolution dump is not a safe rate: step 8 costs
about what step 1 costs, so the answer to "is there a safe rate" is about
requests per second, not about pixels. And a fix, if one is ever wanted, is a
flush scoped to the rows the request will actually return rather than the
whole buffer.

## 3. THE RATE IN THE DESCRIPTION IS TOO HIGH, AND IT VARIES A LOT

"About one displaced band per four whole reads" (0.28 per read) was the
original boot. It did not reproduce at that rate. Measured on this boot, all
at the same divider and the same build:

  145 rounds of the original probe pattern, step 1        0.041 per read
  145 rounds of the same pattern, step 8                  0.028 per read
   80 paced reads, step 1 alone, one every 1.5 s          0.000
   80 paced reads, step 8 alone, one every 1.5 s          0.000
   80 paced reads, step 1 alone, crescent resident        0.000
  120 s idle control, no reads at all                     0.000

So the disturbance is real and the idle control is clean, but the per-read
cost ranges from 0 to 0.28 across conditions on one board. The original
figure should be read as an upper bound seen once, not as the rate.

Two conditions that turned out not to explain the spread. The resident
animation does not: crescent (id 22, band_us 31.9 ms whole frame, the most
expensive in the fleet) produced zero over 80 reads. The step does not, as
above. What does separate the zero arms from the non-zero ones is the round
shape: the arms that produced resyncs bracketed each framebuffer read with
two small JSON GETs and ran about one round every 2.5 s, and the arms that
produced none issued the framebuffer read alone every 1.5 s. That is a faster
framebuffer rate producing fewer resyncs, so it is not the framebuffer rate
that governs it. Not chased further here.

One limit worth recording: the original boot's resyncs began at 250 s of
uptime and none of these arms ran that early, because reproducing that would
have cost a reboot and the board was wanted for other work.

2026-10-01, bench board, divider 6 live (50.7 fps), loadtest build with 6.8
days of uptime, counters from /api/debug/scanout, 100 requests per arm at one
every 2.5 s unless stated. This supersedes section 2 above: the cause is not
the framebuffer endpoint at all.

  arm                                             resyncs   per request
  heap, fb step 1, anim per round (gm-t9ld shape)       5        0.050
  heap, fb step 8, anim per round                       9        0.090
  fb step 1 alone, one every 1.5 s, 80 reads            0        0.000
  /api/debug/heap alone                                 4        0.040
  /api/debug/anim alone                                 0        0.000
  idle control, 120 s                                   0        0.000

slips stayed 0 in every arm. The framebuffer dump, flush included, displaces
nothing on its own in 180 whole reads. The displaced bands belong to
/api/debug/heap: heap_caps_get_largest_free_block walks every block of both
heaps under the heap lock, and the handler's own comment already says about
1.3 ms and one displaced frame per call. Every arm in this bead's history that
produced resyncs bracketed its framebuffer read with a heap GET; every arm
that did not produced zero. That also explains why step 8 was no cheaper than
step 1 (same number of heap GETs) and why a faster unbracketed read rate gave
fewer resyncs. The two previous conclusions, "the flush is the cause" and
"the round shape governs it", were both the heap poll.

Acceptance, as it stands: the bytes are the bytes written (sections 1 and the
576,000 gradient samples with 0 mismatches); only the scan-out is disturbed,
and not by the dump; rates at two or more request rates are above; slips 0
at every rate. CLAUDE.md's framebuffer guidance now carries the table's
conclusion and the "a dump is not atomic" caveat. No closed bead is affected.
Nothing in the firmware changes: the heap endpoint's cost is documented in its
handler and it is a debug route nobody polls in production.
close_reason: Settled on the board 2026-10-01: the dump's bytes are unaffected and the dump itself displaces nothing (180 whole reads, 0 resyncs); the bands came from the probe's /api/debug/heap polls (heap walk under the heap lock, 0.04 per request). slips 0 at every rate. CLAUDE.md framebuffer guidance updated.

title: Fix the Speed law on the animations whose slider does not scale movement
description: Eight animations cannot be calibrated by rescaling because their Speed parameter does not scale movement: Plasma (id 0), Ripples (5), Orbits (8), Silk 2 (13), Horizon (15), Chevrons (17), Refraction (20), Kaleido (25). Evidence and per animation reasons in the gm-33fm notes and in tmp/motion/calibration_plan.json. Done when each one's Speed parameter moves the measured half change time across a range comparable to the fleet's universal curve (about 0.15x to 6.7x from Speed 0 to 100), with 50 near the 1.2 s target; Ripples no longer empties the screen at high settings; Orbits keeps enough frame to frame overlap at Speed 50 to read as travel rather than a dotted trail; Kaleido moves with sub pixel precision instead of whole pixel jumps; the page entry and the firmware port get the same change and still agree pixel for pixel; goldens regenerated; make check, interlace, shapes, fuzz and lifecycle clean.
notes:
Add Truchet (id 30) to this bead, 2026-09-12. The speed calibration slowed it to 0.48x, and at the new rate it advances 0.58 and 0.38 pixels per 66 ms row refresh, so about 28 percent of refreshes repeat the previous picture exactly where none did before. The cal-2 lane reports this is inherent to slowing a whole pixel scroll and that no choice of rate constant avoids it. That is the same defect Kaleido already has in this bead, which moves on 32 percent of steps, and it has the same fix: carry the scroll offset with fractional bits and interpolate, rather than rounding to a whole pixel. Kaleido's is pre-existing and Truchet's was introduced by the calibration, so Truchet is the one to weigh against simply running it faster again. Both are visible as stutter rather than as slowness, which is why the movement metric does not catch them: the mean change per frame is correct while the motion is not smooth.

Add Dimples (id 42) to this bead, 2026-09-12, and correct the scope.

Dimples was classed leave in calibration_plan.json because the movement survey ran
while it was still a placeholder entry, so the calibration never rescaled it. At the
shipped default it measures 3836 ms half change, the slowest in the fleet after nothing.
It is a plain rescale of about 3.2x, not a law fix, and its curve shape above Speed 25
is already close to the universal one.

Current state of the ten animations in scope, measured 2026-09-12 after the gm-33fm
landing (tmp/motion/final50.json). Speed 50 half change, metric as recorded per
animation, target 1200 ms, accept band 950 to 1500:

  Dimples 3836 out   Kaleido 3316 out   Silk 2 3290 out
  Ripples 118 out    Orbits 119 out
  Refraction 1331 in Horizon 1297 in    Chevrons 1180 in
  Truchet 1117 in    Plasma 1055 in

So five are outside the band and five are inside it but have a slider that covers far
too little range. The universal curve the rest of the fleet now follows is
rate = 2^((sp - 50) / 18.2), which puts the target half change at 8050 ms at Speed 0,
3120 at 25, 1200 at 50, 463 at 75 and 179 at 100.

Three lanes launched 2026-09-12 against anims/astra head 8eb6a891, briefs in
tmp/motion/fixlaw_brief.md and fixlaw1.json, fixlaw2.json, fixlaw3.json:

  fixlaw1  Ripples, Orbits. Both about ten times too fast at 50 and neither fixable by
           rescaling. Ripples has a U shaped curve because Speed 100 empties the screen
           and a still picture scores as slow. Orbits is already aliasing at 50, with
           about 0.7 percent lit pixel overlap between consecutive frames.
  fixlaw2  Kaleido, Truchet, Silk 2. The two whole pixel scrollers get a fractional
           scroll offset with interpolation. Silk 2 is too slow everywhere and its
           curve reverses between 50 and 75.
  fixlaw3  Plasma, Horizon, Chevrons, Refraction, Dimples. Four keep their Speed 50
           rate and get the universal curve in place of a private law; Dimples is the
           rescale.

All three lanes landed 2026-09-12: 2489ce26 (fixlaw3), 2aeeb8c7 (fixlaw2), e3a74acd
(fixlaw1). Every one of the ten animations now follows the universal curve and sits in
the band at Speed 50. Half change time in ms at Speed 0, 25, 50, 75, 100, against
targets of 8050, 3120, 1200, 463 and 179:

  Plasma      7894  2884  1055   325   150
  Horizon     7555  3042  1297   412   182
  Chevrons    9078  3367  1180   411   180
  Refraction  7241  4194  1331   638   180
  Dimples     7895  3177  1170   465   188
  Kaleido     5742  3093  1276   381   177
  Truchet     7187  2833  1135   499   199
  Silk 2      8767  3240   988   556   271
  Orbits      6058  3127  1079   547   191   low pass metric
  Ripples     5667  2712  1028   421   339

All monotonic. The two whole pixel scrollers are fixed by carrying the scroll with
fraction bits and reading bilinearly: Kaleido's repeat fraction went from 68 percent of
66 ms steps to zero, Truchet's from 28 percent to zero. Orbits' consecutive frame
overlap of lit pixels went from 0.7 percent to 69 percent, so a body travels instead of
leaving a dotted trail. Ripples no longer empties the screen at high settings: rings now
live 8 times the Fade span whatever the speed and fade over the last 40 percent of it.

Two results outside the 1.6x tolerance, both recorded rather than chased. Ripples at
Speed 100 reads 339 ms against 179 and at Speed 0 reads 5667 against 8050, because the
metric's saturation level is inflated when rings sweep and grow: two moments then differ
more by how much ring there is than by where it is. Against the curve's own plateau the
rings move half way in about 160 ms. Silk 2 at 100 reads 271 against 179, and its sheen
was deliberately left on its old rate because scaling that too put Speed 50 at 560 ms and
put the reversal back.

One regression, measured on the host, 600 frames, the commit against its parent:
Truchet's band cost doubled, 0.155 ms to 0.320. Kaleido's bilinear is free because it
lives in frame() and the band still reads a prepared field; Truchet's assembles two tile
rows and blends per row inside band(), which runs 240 times a frame. Silk 2 unchanged at
0.079. On the device Truchet's band was 17,268 us with its kernel, so at 2x it lands near
Nebula at 33,847, the heaviest in the fleet, on a whole frame path where a frame's work
already exceeds one panel period. The fixlaw2 lane has been asked whether a cheaper shape
keeps the repeat fraction at zero: moving the vertical blend to frame(), interpolating
only the faster axis, or caching the two tile rows across the bands of one frame. This
needs a device measurement either way and belongs on gm-3vj.47.

Side effect worth recording: replacing Plasma's private speed law with the fleet curve
also closed its page against firmware gap, 10,538 differing pixels to zero, because the
two sides had been carrying different arithmetic for the same thing. A divergence can be
a symptom of something else rather than its own bug.

Round two, 2026-09-12. A full fleet sweep after round one landed, at Speed 0, 25, 50,
75 and 100, found fourteen more animations whose slider does not cover the fleet's
range. Round one only ever looked at the ten the original survey named, and the survey
measured Speed 50 alone, so nothing had ever swept the other thirty-four.

Worst ratio against the universal curve, and where it falls, at head d9f8d38d:

  Saddle       4.45x at 100    8014  2473  1316   898   797
  Brushed      4.32x at 100    7082  1961  1478   763   773   not monotonic
  Sundial      3.75x at 100    7726  2362  1475   936   672
  Crescent     3.34x at 100    7580  1944  1180   903   597
  Oculus       3.03x at 100    5602  1317  1090   647   543
  Mosaic       2.99x at 100    8323  2357  1152   924   536
  Steam        2.69x at 100    3294  1983  1194   763   482
  Glint        2.68x at 100    4145  1345  1010   495   480
  Ember        1.84x at 75    10474  4310  1135   251   262   not monotonic
  Caustics     1.73x at 0      4648  2374  1041   417   169
  Harmonograph 1.71x at 0      4700  2754  1281   480   168
  Stripes      1.69x at 100    8787  3425  1079   531   302
  Tide         1.64x at 75     5309  2804  1212   283   247
  Grid, Quilt, Shafts sit at 1.55 to 1.59, just inside.

Targets are 8050, 3120, 1200, 463 and 179 ms, tolerance a factor of 1.6 at the ends
and the 950 to 1500 band at 50.

Every one of these is inside the band at Speed 50, so the movement the owner asked
about is right and only the slider is wrong. Eight of the thirteen are flat at the top
in exactly the way Plasma, Horizon, Chevrons and Refraction were: a private affine law
of the shape a + p0 * b / 100 covering two or three times where the fleet covers 54.
Glint's last quarter of slider buys 1.03x and does nothing at all.

Two shapes are new. Caustics and Harmonograph are wrong only at the bottom, about 1.7
times too fast at Speed 0 with everything above Speed 25 already in tolerance, which no
animation in round one did. Ember and Tide are too steep in the middle and then flat or
reversed at the top.

Three lanes launched against d9f8d38d, briefs in tmp/motion/fixlaw_round2.md and
fixlaw4.json, fixlaw5.json, fixlaw6.json: fixlaw4 has Saddle, Brushed, Sundial and
Crescent; fixlaw5 has Oculus, Mosaic, Glint and Ember; fixlaw6 has Caustics,
Harmonograph, Stripes and Tide. Steam is left out because the pciz4 lane holds that
file, and it needs a later pass.

The round-two brief carries what round one taught: anchor at Speed 50 and do not move
it, look for the affine law before hunting a saturating term, a speed law belongs in
frame() and not in band(), and some targets cannot be reached because the metric
saturates rather than because the animation is wrong.

Device round, 2026-09-12, bench board at 192.168.1.121, display-loadtest, stored
pixel-clock divider 7, whole-frame path, cap 60. Stored settings left as found.

The Truchet blend-in-frame change was verified on the board and it is not the
regression the host predicted. Three runs of tools/framefn_sweep.py on each of
two builds that differ only in AnimTruchet.cpp (2aeeb8c7 against HEAD), ms per
whole frame:

  before   framefn 0.1   band 21.4   work 32.5   19.2 fps
  after    framefn 4.4   band 18.6   work 33.0   19.4 fps

So the move trades 4.4 ms of once-a-frame setup for 2.8 ms of band work, total
work is flat inside run-to-run noise, and the frame rate did not move. The host
measured the same change as a 32 percent rise because it counts arithmetic; the
device band path is bus bound and what it saves is the PSRAM traffic of the
rows it no longer blends. /api/debug/animtest agrees: band_us 357,541 before
and 310,402 after, a 13 percent drop over the same 5,760 bands.

Finding it cost the board twice. /api/debug/animtest on Truchet rebooted it
every time, with `assert failed: multi_heap_free ... head != NULL` and a
backtrace ending in the animation's own release(). The cause was blendLast, the
table the change added: a PIE store destination taken from bganim::alloc(),
which called ps_malloc and so promised four-byte alignment, while ee.vst.128.ip
zeroes the low four address bits of its own access. Every vector store landed
up to twelve bytes before the block, on the heap's head canary. Fixed in
2e2beebb by aligning inside alloc() rather than at the one table, so no
animation can get an unaligned table from bganim at all. CLAUDE.md carries the
rule under the ee.vld/vst bullet.

Worth knowing: the host cannot see this class of bug. glibc malloc is 16-byte
aligned, so the goldens, the fuzzer, the lifecycle check and QEMU all agreed
with a device that was writing outside its allocation.

Fleet state on the shipped build, after all four lanes landed: /api/debug/animtest
clean for all 44 animations, mismatch 0 each, no init failures, no reboot.
Scan-out slips 0, hot_fail 0, int_free 26,995, dma_min 12,700.

Round two landed 2026-09-12 (89b6ba7e, 8e394fbb, 5054f174): Saddle, Brushed,
Sundial, Crescent, Oculus, Mosaic, Glint, Ember and Caustics.

Speed 50 is now done. All 44 animations sit inside the 950 to 1500 ms band,
median 1180 ms against the 1200 ms target, spread 1.5x. It was 144x before any
of this work and 32.5x after round one.

The slider range is not done. A five point sweep of the whole fleet at Speed 0,
25, 50, 75 and 100 against the curve rate = 2^((sp - 50) / 18.2), tolerance a
factor of 1.6, puts 35 of 44 inside at every stop. Nine are out, with the stop
that fails and the factor:

  Steam         2.69x at 100   3294 1983 1194  763  482
  Glint         2.56x at 100   4077 1972 1010  256   70
  Oculus        2.18x at 100   5542 3050 1090  484   82
  Ripples       1.89x at 100   5667 2712 1028  421  339
  Ember         1.84x at  75  10474 4310 1135  251  262
  Brushed       1.76x at  75   7249 3444 1478  817  231
  Harmonograph  1.71x at   0   4700 2754 1281  480  168
  Stripes       1.69x at 100   8787 3425 1079  531  302
  Tide          1.64x at  75   5309 2804 1212  283  247

Targets are 8050 3120 1200 463 179. Two shapes of failure, and they need
different fixes. Steam, Ripples, Stripes and Tide flatten at the top: some
motion term does not read Speed at all, so the fast end cannot get fast.
Glint and Oculus now overshoot at the top, 70 and 82 ms against 179, which
round two introduced: a term got the multiplier twice, or got a steeper one.
Ember and Tide are non-monotonic between 75 and 100, which means a term wraps
or clamps.

Harmonograph is the only one that fails at the slow end, and it fails alone
because its curve is rasterised rather than sampled.

fixlaw6 was asked for Caustics, Harmonograph, Stripes and Tide and delivered
Caustics only, so three of the nine above are that lane's unfinished work.

Round three, 2026-09-12, done in this session rather than in a lane.

Two of the nine were real defects and both are fixed. Steam scaled its rise
and nothing else, so a fast setting shortened the plume instead of speeding it
up (92b95cf7). Ripples scaled the ring travel but not the drop interval or the
ring life, so Speed 100 showed less movement than Speed 75 (9a512956). Both
now measure inside the tolerance and both leave the Speed 50 picture exactly
where it was, so the goldens and the page allowances did not move.

The other seven are Glint, Oculus, Ember, Brushed, Harmonograph, Stripes and
Tide, and reading the code says the law is already right in all seven: each
multiplies one clock, which every motion reads, by speedMul(p[0]). What fails
is the measurement, not the animation. The half change time divides the
one-step change by an estimate of "fully changed", and that estimate is
unreliable for a near-periodic picture, exactly as MOTION.md warns for Ripples
and Steam. The Glint kernel comment already records an instance: slowing that
animation by 1.53x measured 9 percent faster.

The check that does not need the estimate is chg66, the fraction of pixels
that change in one 66 ms step. All seven rise at every stop of the slider, so
the picture really does speed up:

  Ember          0.13   0.28   0.70   2.42  15.27 percent
  Brushed        1.02   2.94   4.75  15.16  33.20
  Oculus         0.71   1.64   3.85  12.58  33.13
  Glint          8.17  11.65  27.09  42.13  52.63
  Tide           1.28   5.90  18.42  42.22  64.65
  Stripes        0.27   0.89   1.92   5.38  30.09
  Harmonograph   1.77   3.53   5.86   6.72   7.85

That is also how the two real defects were told apart from the seven: Steam
and Ripples were the only ones whose chg66 did not rise all the way.
Harmonograph is the weakest of the seven, 4.4x across a 45x rate range,
because what its picture shows is a dense rasterised curve whose coverage
looks much the same once the phase advances more than a stamp per frame.

Fleet state. Speed 50: 44 of 44 inside the 950 to 1500 ms band, median 1180 ms
against a 1200 ms target, spread 1.5x, from 144x before any of this work.
Across the slider at Speed 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100: 37 of 44 within a factor of
1.6 of the curve, the other seven above.

What would close this bead, and it is the owner's call which: accept the seven
on the chg66 evidence, or give motion.js a saturation estimate a near-periodic
picture does not fool, in which case measure the seven again first, since the
fix may be in the instrument rather than in any animation.

Closed 2026-09-12. The seven that the wall-clock sweep still put outside the curve
were a measurement artefact, and the instrument now says so directly. motion.js
takes --matched: it divides every playback time by the setting's rate, so each Speed
plays the same window of animation time, and reports thalfAdjMs with the rate
multiplied back. An animation whose Speed is one multiplier on one clock reads the
same adjusted value at every setting, and no saturation estimate enters the
comparison.

That sweep found five animations that really did leave a term unscaled, three of
which had passed every check the fleet had:

  Steam      scaled the rise and not the puff lifetime or the sway
  Ripples    scaled the ring travel and not the drop interval or the ring life
  Starfield  scaled the star drift and not the shooting star clock
  Lava       scaled one of two clocks
  Silk       scaled the base frequency and not the per wave wobble

All five are fixed (92b95cf7, 9a512956, 798b3d28), page mirrors with them, and the
Speed 50 picture is untouched in every case, so no golden and no page allowance
moved. The final matched sweep reads 44 of 44 flat within 2 percent, worst 1.017x
(Quilt and Oculus). Speed 50 stays 44 of 44 in the 950 to 1500 band, median 1180 ms,
spread 1.5x.

The five clock fixes were verified on the bench board after the flash of 798b3d28:
/api/debug/animtest clean for all 44, mismatch 0 each, no init failures, sc_slips 0,
hot_fail 0, internal free 27,587 B, DMA low-water 16,199 B, divider 7.

The instrument change is 6b141989, with MOTION.md carrying when to use --matched and
when not: a matched run answers whether the slider scales the whole clock, a
wall-clock run answers how fast the picture actually moves, and reading one as the
other is what cost a day here.

title: Grind screen: a content-sized weight label re-flows its flex row on every update
description:
The grind screen publishes 3.4 times a second while a weight is moving, and
0.00 when it is not. Bench board, divider 6, whole-frame path, synthetic scale
at 0.5 g/s, three 20 s windows back to back: ramp 0 gives 0.00, ramp 0.5 gives
3.43, ramp 0 gives 0.00 again. Every one of the screen's three text elements is
owned throughout and text_dbg reports zero refusals and zero releases, so this
is not a compositor element losing its label.

What invalidates is the flex layout. objects.mode_switch1 (screens.c, the grind
screen) is a 160x50 container with LV_LAYOUT_FLEX, LV_FLEX_FLOW_ROW and
LV_FLEX_ALIGN_SPACE_EVENLY. Its two children are objects.obj24, the tare
imgbtn, and objects.obj25, the weight label, and obj25 is LV_SIZE_CONTENT wide.
So every digit-width change ("5.4g" to "26.8g" to "-3.4g") re-flows the row and
moves both children. lv_flex.c:522-529 invalidates a moved child's old box and
then its new box, which is four invalidations per weight update, and none of
them is covered by the compositor-owner patches: scripts/patch_lvgl_label_elem.py
guards lv_label's own invalidations and lv_obj_pos's size and move ones for a
USER_2 label, and flex invalidates the item directly. The imgbtn is not a label
at all, so no label patch could ever reach it.

Read off /api/debug/anim with invmin=8, callers resolved against the ELF: the
ring is the same four entries repeating, an object at 50x50 near x 167 to 171
and a label at 83 to 95 px wide near x 222 to 230, each at lv_flex.c:527 and
lv_flex.c:529.

The guard in lv_flex is correct (if(diff_x || diff_y)), so there is nothing to
fix in LVGL. The fix is to stop the row re-flowing: give obj25 a fixed width so
its box does not change with the digits. That is what buildScaleScreen already
does for the scale cover's readout, which is 170 px wide and right-aligned for
this exact reason (CLAUDE.md, UI-pipeline invariants). obj25 is generated code,
so the width belongs in DefaultUI::tuneGeneratedScreen with the other
generated-screen patches, not in screens.c. It moves the number's resting
position slightly, so it is the owner's call.

Checked and not affected: every other content-sized label inside a flex
container (brew profile_name and obj4, profile_screen obj18/21/22/23,
new_profile's four phase labels) changes on a profile switch, not on telemetry,
so none is on a per-value path. The brew screen carries a weight readout too and
measures 0.00 with the same ramp, because its label is not laid out by flex.
notes: Decided 2026-10-01, owner delegated the default: obj25 keeps its content width. The churn is 3.4 publishes a second only while a weight is moving on the grind screen, and the fix (a fixed width in tuneGeneratedScreen, as the scale cover's 170 px readout has) moves the resting position of the number, which the owner has not seen. The mechanism and the fix are recorded in CLAUDE.md (UI-pipeline invariants, gm-nly bullet) and tools/inval_sweep.py reproduces it with /api/debug/scale?ramp=0.5. Closed as accepted; reopen when the grind screen layout is next touched.

title: Unexplained brew-screen churn on a board in the gm-t9ld degraded state
description:
A per-screen sweep on 2026-09-15 read the brew screen at 3.56 overlay publishes
a second and the grind screen at 3.19, on a board with 2.6 hours of uptime. The
sweep's own health check (three small GETs) passed at its start; the next
script's health check, minutes later, failed, which is the gm-t9ld degraded
radio state. After a hard reset with no flash the same script on the same binary
read brew 0.10 and grind 0.48.

Grind is explained and has its own bead (gm-nly): a synthetic scale ramp was
still running from an earlier script, and a moving weight re-flows that screen's
flex row. Brew is not explained. With the same ramp on a healthy board the brew
screen measures 0.00, checked twice, so the ramp does not account for it.

Why this matters beyond one bad reading. Overlay publishes are counted on the
device and the rate is computed from the device's own uptime_ms, so a stalling
radio cannot inflate the number the way it inflates an HTTP timing. If the
elevated rate really does belong to the degraded window, then whatever gm-t9ld
is reaches further than the radio, and a device-side counter is a second way to
see it. The alternative is that some other state cleared on the reset and the
timing with gm-t9ld is a coincidence. Nothing here separates the two.

What to capture next time, so the question is answerable rather than argued:
tools/churn_sweep.py now prints text_dbg (element takes, refusals, releases)
and the glyph atlas figures next to every rate, and says whether any label
actually changed during the window. A refusal is sticky for the rest of a screen
visit, so a single one explains a screen that churns for as long as it is up;
both counters read zero on the healthy board. The atlas was ruled out directly:
19 glyphs in 3,397 bytes of a 32 KB per-font arena after cycling every screen,
so it was nowhere near full.

The board reached the degraded state again about 15 minutes after that reset,
during a session doing frequent small GETs.

title: More gradients, grouped into categories
description:
Grow the built-in gradient set from 18 to about 60 and group it into eight categories, on both the web tab and the display.

Decided by the owner on 2026-09-12:

- About 60 gradients in all, roughly seven or eight per category.
- Categories are mood and subject, not hue family: Coffee, Fire and Heat, Water and Ice, Nature, Night Sky, Neon, Pastel, Metal and Stone.
- The display picks from a child page with swatches, not from a longer prev and next cycle.
- Storage keeps the decimal index and the table stays append only. Categories are metadata on a gradient, never a reordering.

## Why this is more than adding table entries

Four copies of the theme table existed and were synced by hand: THEMES in BgAnimThemes.cpp, BG_THEMES in web/src/config/bgAnimations.js, kSimThemeNames in CatAnimation.cpp, and THEME_NAMES in tools/settings_ui_tests/test_animation.py.

gm-nov3.1 replaced the first three handwritten copies with two generated outputs. The runner's handwritten copy is gm-nov3.8. At 60 entries, drift could make a picker name one gradient while the panel draws another.

bgAnimGradientRef and every slot of bgAnimThemeMap store a decimal array index such as "7", not a slug. Existing entries must never move.

The display currently cycles through a default choice, 18 built-ins and up to 12 saved gradients. The arrows wrap and repeat on hold. The reason to replace them is to show each gradient before choosing it and make a larger collection easy to browse.

All 18 built-ins are dark-to-bright ramps. Keep that design policy for the expanded set. It is not a renderer restriction: saved gradients can have other shapes, and Plasma builds a cyclic palette.

## Legacy compatibility

The legacy integer bgAnimTheme uses 18 for the old single custom gradient. The current resolver and migration derive that sentinel from the table length, so appending entries changes its meaning.

gm-nov3.7 must land before gm-nov3.5. It freezes the historical legacy meaning, separates explicit decimal refs from legacy integers, and makes migration safe with existing selections, full libraries and partial persistence failures. Production entries cannot be appended before it lands.

An explicit ref "18" on the expanded build selects built-in 18. Legacy integer 18 continues to mean Custom, with built-in 0 as the fallback for an empty or invalid custom string.

## Where the 18 already sit

Coffee 1 (Espresso), Fire and Heat 3 (Sunset, Fire, Ember Coal), Water and Ice 4 (Ocean, Ice, Teal Reef, Arctic Night), Nature 2 (Forest, Lime), Night Sky 3 (Violet Dusk, Aurora, Deep Space), Neon 1 (Cyber), Pastel 2 (Rose, Sakura), Metal and Stone 2 (Mono, Gold).

Coffee and Neon need the most new entries.

Earlier review measurements recorded a median mean CIEDE2000 distance of 26.5 across the 153 pairs, with nine pairs below 10: Forest and Lime 4.26, Rose and Sakura 4.28, Ocean and Ice 6.23, Espresso and Fire 6.94, Sunset and Fire 8.80, Forest and Aurora 9.14, Ice and Arctic Night 9.61, Violet Dusk and Cyber 9.78, Espresso and Gold 9.97.

Those figures are background evidence of crowding, not the thresholds for a different sampling method. gm-nov3.4 fixes the evaluation settings and derives the baseline exemptions under its actual metric. New gradients cannot expand that exemption list.

## Accepted consequences

Writers mirror built-ins 0 to 17 unchanged into bgAnimTheme and mirror newer built-ins as 0.

On rollback to an 18-theme build, an explicit global ref above 17 does not resolve and falls through to the legacy mirror. A newly selected global built-in above 17 therefore falls back to Espresso on that older build. The explicit ref remains stored and resolves again after upgrade.

A per-animation override above 17 falls through to the global on the older build. Its result depends on that global, including the legacy mirror when needed.

Migration preserves existing explicit refs and map slots. A legacy Custom that cannot be migrated safely remains supported through the legacy path.

Gradients cannot be removed or reordered. A future removal scheme could add a ref form such as "t:<slug>" and preserve the old decimal lookup table. That scheme is outside this epic.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] gm-nov3.2 through gm-nov3.8 meet their acceptance criteria, with gm-nov3.1 remaining the completed generation baseline.
- [ ] The final generated tables agree with data/gradients.json and preserve all original indices, names and stops.
- [ ] Both settings surfaces expose the grouped collection, and the display uses the child-page swatch picker.
- [ ] Recorded upgrade and rollback tests match the legacy and explicit-ref rules above.
close_reason: Every child bead is closed (the last, gm-nov3.38, on 2026-10-01 at f0db1611 on anims/astra); the gradient decisions gm-2tqj and gm-ryny stay open as the owner's calls

title: One source file and a generator for the three gradient tables
description:
One source file for the built-in gradients, and a generator that writes every
table that reads it. No new gradients and no behaviour change in this bead:
the generated tables must be byte-for-byte equivalent to what the three
hand-written copies hold today.

Today the same 18 gradients are written out three times and kept in step by
hand:

- `THEMES[]` in `src/display/ui/default/bganim/BgAnimThemes.cpp`
- `BG_THEMES` in `web/src/config/bgAnimations.js`
- `kSimThemeNames[]` in `src/display/ui/default/settings/CatAnimation.cpp`,
  because `BgAnimThemes.cpp` is excluded under `GAGGIMATE_SIM`

## Shape

`data/gradients.json`: an ordered array of `{ name, category, stops }`, six
`#rrggbb` stops each, in the order the firmware table has them today, so every
index keeps the gradient it has now.

`scripts/gen_gradients.py` writes, all checked in:

- `src/display/ui/default/bganim/BgAnimThemeTable.h`, the `Theme` array
  `BgAnimThemes.cpp` includes
- `src/display/ui/default/bganim/BgAnimThemeNames.h`, names and categories
  only, with no stops, for the simulator to include in place of its mirror
- `web/src/config/bgThemes.js`, exporting `BG_THEMES`, which
  `bgAnimations.js` re-exports so no importer changes

Checked in rather than generated at build time, because the firmware build,
the web build and the host tests all read them and none of the three should
need Python.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `data/gradients.json` holds the 18 gradients in their current order,
      with the categories the epic lists.
- [ ] `python3 scripts/gen_gradients.py` regenerates all three outputs, and
      running it twice leaves the tree unchanged.
- [ ] `scripts/gen_gradients.py --check` exits non-zero when a generated file
      differs from what the source would produce, and is wired into
      `tools/animbench` `make check`.
- [ ] The generated `THEMES[]` stops are byte-identical to the current
      hand-written table (compare the compiled rodata, or diff the generated
      header against the extracted current table).
- [ ] `BG_THEMES` in the generated JS is deep-equal to the current array,
      including stop strings and order.
- [ ] `kSimThemeNames[]` is deleted and `CatAnimation.cpp` uses the generated
      names header under `GAGGIMATE_SIM`.
- [ ] `pio run -e display`, `-e display-loadtest` and `-e display-sim` build.
- [ ] `pio test -e native_settingsui` passes unchanged.
- [ ] `tools/settings_ui_test.py --only animation` on the simulator passes
      unchanged.
- [ ] The generator rejects a source entry that is not exactly six stops, or
      whose stops are not valid `#rrggbb`.
notes:
Done in 8f61e73a.

`data/gradients.json` is the only place a built-in gradient is written. It
carries the category list and, per gradient, name, category and six stops.
`scripts/gen_gradients.py` writes two checked-in outputs:

- `src/display/ui/default/bganim/BgAnimThemeTable.h`, which
  `BgAnimThemes.cpp`'s `THEMES` now points at through
  `using Theme = bganim_gen::ThemeDef;`
- `web/src/config/bgThemes.js`, which `bgAnimations.js` imports and
  re-exports, so every importer of `BG_THEMES` is untouched

One generated header rather than the two the plan named: the simulator does
not need a stops-free table, it is a host build. It includes the same header,
under `#ifdef GAGGIMATE_SIM`, and `kSimThemeNames[]` is deleted. Device builds
must not include it, or they pull the stops in twice.

`--check` fails on a stale copy and runs first in `tools/animbench` `make
check`.

The generator rejects an entry that is not exactly six lower-case `#rrggbb`
stops, a duplicate name, or a category the file does not declare. It does not
and cannot enforce append-only, because that is a property of history, not of
the file.

## Proof of no behaviour change

`tools/.../verify_identical.py` (kept in the job scratch, not the repo) parses
three things out of git at HEAD before this commit, the C table, the JS mirror
and the deleted simulator mirror, and compares all three against the generated
pair, name for name and stop for stop. Result: IDENTICAL, 18 entries on every
side, and the simulator mirror's order matched.

Deliberately breaking one generated file makes `--check` exit 1 and name the
file; regenerating makes it exit 0.

## Checks run

- `pio test -e native_settingsui`: 37 cases pass.
- `pio run -e display-sim`: SUCCESS.
- `pio run -e display-loadtest`: SUCCESS, 5m20s.
- `tools/settings_ui_test.py --only animation,rig` on the simulator: PASS,
  animation 93 checks, rig 19, four animation pages audited clean, smallest
  target 56x56 px.
- `npm run lint:check` clean for these files, prettier clean, `npm run build`
  clean.
- `-e display` not built here: the worktree's libdeps for that env do not
  install on WSL1 (CLAUDE.md). The change is identical across envs and
  display-loadtest compiles the same sources.

## Category split of the 18

Coffee 1, Fire and Heat 3, Water and Ice 4, Nature 2, Night Sky 3, Neon 1,
Pastel 2, Metal and Stone 2. Nothing reads the category yet; that is gm-nov3.2.

## Correction, 2026-09-12

This bead and its commit message both say three hand-synced copies. There were
four. The fourth is `THEME_NAMES` in
`tools/settings_ui_tests/test_animation.py`, an 18-name list in table order,
and this bead did not touch it. Generating it is gm-nov3.8, which blocks
gm-nov3.5 because the runner's index-to-name mapping goes wrong above index 17
as soon as the table grows.

title: Implement and run the deferred gradient framebuffer comparison
description:
Commit 71bd9f20 closed gm-nov3.4 with its controlled device comparison unfinished. tools/gradient_sheet.py documents a proposed fixture, but provides no executable fixture or recorded comparison. gm-nov3.5 requires that controlled method for reviewing an appended batch.

Implement a reusable bench-only fixture and host comparison. Render known ramp indices through production palette arithmetic, with matched stops, uniform or positional semantics, brightness, highlight rolloff and gain. Keep overlays and other compositing effects out of the sampled region.

Use the existing rendering ownership rules in CLAUDE.md. The HTTP task must not paint directly into a framebuffer. Record the actual fixture command and pixel-to-ramp mapping.

The previous no-flash restriction was a valid reason to defer execution. This follow-up retains the unfinished acceptance work.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A bench-only fixture renders known palette indices and reports the stops, interpolation mode, tone settings, gain and sampled region.
- [ ] A host command reads /api/debug/fb and compares individual RGB565 samples with the tested JS sampler, exiting non-zero on a mismatch.
- [ ] A recorded device run covers a six-stop built-in at 100/100 and 60/65 tone settings, including ramp index 255.
- [ ] The record includes firmware identity, commands, sample mapping, compared sample count and mismatch count.
- [ ] tools/gradient_sheet.py documents the implemented command and result instead of leaving only a proposed design.
- [ ] The command is reusable for the batch comparison required by gm-nov3.5.
notes:
Done in commit f580985a on anims/astra. All six acceptance criteria checked.

WHAT WAS BUILT

Fixture: /api/debug/gradfix, GM_TOUCH_PROBE builds only, in the real-panel
block of WebUIPluginDebug.cpp. Arms a ramp strip that the render task paints
into rows [y0, y1) of every band, after every compositing stage and before the
push, so no overlay, layer, element or scrim reaches the sampled rows. The HTTP
task paints nothing: it sets three atomics. Interlacing is vetoed while armed,
because an interlaced frame writes only one of the two framebuffers.

Arguments: on=0|1|2|3 (off, ramp, reversed, wheel), y0=, y1=, xoff=0|1,
btone=/ktone= (a held tone in percent, -1 releases), stops=<wire>&anim=N (an
arbitrary gradient through the editor's live-preview path; empty ends it).
Nothing is persisted and nothing writes NVS.

Report: firmware version and build time, armed, mode, frames painted, y0, y1,
x0, x1, w, h, xoff, the mapping in words, gain256, brightness256, knee,
brightnessPct, kneePct, toneOverride, stopCount, uniform, themeGen, and the
stops BEFORE tone as the firmware's own wire format. Two new reporting
accessors in BgAnimCommon (themeRawStops, themeToneState) are where the
pre-tone stops and the live tone come from. Nothing is read from /api/settings.

Host command: tools/gradient_fb_check.py. Reads /api/debug/fb, compares
individual RGB565 samples against tools/gradient_samples.js fed with what the
device reported, exits non-zero on a mismatch. --batch walks every entry in
data/gradients.json through the preview path, which is the form gm-nov3.5
needs. --selftest runs two negative controls.

SAMPLE MAPPING

Column x carries ramp index ((x + xoff) * 255) / (w - 1), clamped to 255, and
every row of the strip is painted identically. /api/debug/fb only delivers the
framebuffer subsampled (step 2 on this panel; step 1 truncates after five
rows), so a host reads even columns and would never see column 479 where index
255 sits. Two passes, xoff 0 and 1, cover every column's index: measured
coverage 256 of 256.

THE RECORDED RUN

Board 192.168.1.121, pixel-clock divider 7 (read from /api/debug/pclk before
and after; the build default is 6 and the CLAUDE.md note says 8, so this board
has moved again), whole-frame path, stored settings untouched.

Firmware v1.9.8-sleep9-644-g265501e0, built 2026-09-13T10:09:56Z, for both
records. Re-confirmed afterwards on the committed build
v1.9.8-sleep9-645-gf580985a with the same result.

  python3 tools/gradient_fb_check.py --host 192.168.1.121 \
      --tone 100,100 --tone 60,65 --selftest \
      --json tools/gradient_fb_check/report.json

  Aurora, the six-stop built-in the board had stored, uniform.
  Four passes: two tones x xoff 0 and 1, both framebuffers each.
  38,400 samples compared, 0 mismatches, ramp indices 0 to 255.

  python3 tools/gradient_fb_check.py --host 192.168.1.121 --batch \
      --buffers 0 --tone 100,100 \
      --json tools/gradient_fb_check/batch_report.json

  All 18 built-ins at 100/100, xoff 0 and 1: 172,800 samples, 0 mismatches.

The self test is what makes those zeros evidence. Same armed strip against a
ramp sampled at 50/50: 4,800 mismatches. Correct ramp against the same region
with the fixture off: 4,795. A check that cannot fail proves nothing.

ONE FINDING WORTH KEEPING

/api/debug/fb degrades with uptime. On a board that has just booted it delivers
the whole 240x240 dump; after a few hundred requests it drops the chunked
response partway, at every step value, and internal free has fallen from 30.9
kB to 26.2 with the largest block down from 20.5 kB to 15.9. A reboot restores
it. This is the internal-DRAM starvation symptom CLAUDE.md already describes
for the web UI, reached through the debug endpoints instead. The tool retries
and keeps a short read when it still reaches the strip's rows, so a run
finishes either way, but a long batch wants a reboot first. Not fixed here;
worth its own bead if anyone leans on /api/debug/fb harder.

BUILDS AND CHECKS

pio run -e display-loadtest: SUCCESS (the build flashed).
pio run -e display-sim: SUCCESS.
pio run -e display: not attempted; it does not build in this worktree on WSL1.

CORRECTION, 2026-09-13. The cause named under "ONE FINDING WORTH KEEPING"
is wrong.

That note said /api/debug/fb degrades with uptime and blamed internal DRAM
starvation, on the strength of internal free falling from 30.9 kB to 26.2 kB
and the largest block from 20.5 kB to 15.9 kB while short reads appeared.
Two later investigations say the heap was not the cause.

1. The short step 1 read was a bug in the response filler, not a heap
condition (gm-6ivh, 28cec8ec, 2026-09-13). The filler wrote whole output
rows and returned 0 when the send budget could not hold one, and the web
server reads a 0 as the end of the body. At step 1 a row is 960 bytes and
the first send round's budget always falls below that, so every step 1
request returned exactly 4,800 of 460,800 bytes with a 200 and no error. It
was never heap dependent and never uptime dependent. Step 2 rows are 480
bytes and always fit, which is why only step 1 ever looked broken. That also
retires the line in this bead's SAMPLE MAPPING section saying step 1
truncates after five rows: it does not, since gm-6ivh.

2. The eight minute stall after a flash (gm-t9ld) was not starvation
either. A small JSON GET with no framebuffer in it took 2.03 s in the same
window, so whatever was slow sat in front of both handlers. The heap moved
about 700 bytes between the sick and healthy windows and dma_free never
came near the 1,630 byte WiFi frame copy.

3. The board serves fine on far less internal headroom than it had while it
was stalling. In a warm window during the 2026-09-13 probe runs
int_largest was 8,180 and dma_min had already dipped to 1,207, and every
framebuffer read in that window came back whole and fast (measured by the
agent that ran the same probe earlier that day). gm-t9ld's broken window had
int_largest 15,348 and dma_free 18,191. Less headroom, healthy; more
headroom, stalled. That is the cleanest single argument that internal DRAM
starvation is not what caused the short reads.

A 15 minute run at HEAD on 2026-09-13 (336 rounds, one whole step 1 read
each) read 460,800 bytes every time in 1.22 to 1.78 s with int_largest
pinned at 11,252 throughout, so the uptime dependence described above is
also not reproducible on the fixed build.

Nothing else in this bead changes: the gradient framebuffer check and its
self test stand as recorded.

title: Exercise the declared category order fixture through production accessors

title: Run the frozen sentinel migration on the bench board
description:
Run the legacy custom gradient migration on the bench board. Commit 2fd637eb introduced the frozen sentinel, separate explicit-ref namespace, production migration planner and staged persistence. Its notes report 57 host cases including fault injection and original-table and 60-entry-table fixtures, but no hardware migration run.

The host store does not reproduce NVS itself. In particular, the migration treats an empty-string clear as unverifiable because a failed clear can report success. Hardware evidence must cover the actual stored library, legacy fields and persistence behavior.

The earlier simulator limitation is obsolete. Commits 3b0db5a7 and 265501e0 link the real BgAnimThemes.cpp rules, so a seeded retained fallback can reach Custom (legacy) in the simulator. Boot migration remains excluded by the GAGGIMATE_SIM guard in DefaultUI.cpp:1869, and simulator coverage does not replace this device task.

gm-nov3.10 currently holds the board. Perform this task after that work releases it and device testing is authorized. Read and record settings first. Restore bgAnimTheme, bgAnimCustomTheme, bgAnimGradientRef, bgAnimThemeMap and bgAnimGradients, together with any other changed settings. Never erase NVS. Record the divider from /api/debug/pclk and leave a normal build on the board.

A larger gradient table belongs only in the temporary test build. Do not commit those additions to data/gradients.json.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Set up a device fixture through the web UI: a stored valid custom gradient, legacy bgAnimTheme 18, an empty global ref and a recorded framebuffer of the active fallback.
- [ ] Flash a test build with more than 18 built-ins and compare the resulting gradient through /api/debug/fb using gm-nov3.10's controlled method and matched animation and tone settings.
- [ ] Verify the custom gradient is durably present in the library, the published global c<id> resolves to that entry with the original uniform semantics, and the map is unchanged.
- [ ] Verify a second boot changes no settings and adds no library entry.
- [ ] Verify an already migrated device keeps its selection on another boot and does not reactivate a leftover custom string.
- [ ] Verify a deferred fallback shows Custom (legacy) with its real stops on the panel.
- [ ] Record firmware identities, settings before and after, panel divider, commands and compared sample counts.
- [ ] Leave the board with a normal build and its original stored settings, and record that restoration.
notes:
Done on the bench board 2026-09-13. Record committed in 438aa3fe:
tools/gradient_fb_check/migration_device_run.json (the migration run),
batch60_report.json and selftest60_report.json (the 60 gradient framebuffer
batch and its negative controls). All eight criteria checked.

IDENTITIES AND CONDITIONS

Board 192.168.1.121. Stored pixel-clock divider 7, read from /api/debug/pclk
before and after (the build default is 6, and an older note says 8, so this
board has moved again). bgAnimInterlace is 0, so everything ran on the
whole-frame path.

Firmware before: v1.9.8-sleep9-654-g7d3c8906-dirty, built 2026-09-13T11:32:23Z,
18 built-ins. Firmware after: v1.9.8-sleep9-658-g6a2e910c (HEAD),
display-loadtest, built 2026-09-13T12:05:55Z, 60 built-ins. Flashed with
esptool write-flash 0x10000 firmware.bin, so the app partition only. NVS was
never erased. data/gradients.json was not touched: HEAD already carries 60.

THE MIGRATION

Fixture set through /api/settings with only the gradient fields plus the four
booleans the handler would otherwise clear (homekit and friends are
unconditional setters, so a partial POST would switch them off). Legacy
bgAnimTheme 18, bgAnimCustomTheme
"200a2a@0,4a1060@40,8a2090@90,c04ab0@160,e89a60@210,ffe0a0@255" with explicit
positions, empty bgAnimGradientRef, the board's own two library entries and its
own map left in place.

Before the flash the resolver already reported the stops with the positions
discarded (uniform true), which is the legacy rendering rule. The ramp strip
was captured through /api/debug/gradfix and /api/debug/fb at step 1, full
460,800 byte dumps, 40 identical rows of 480 pixels each.

After the flash, on the first boot of the 60-entry build:

  bgAnimGradients  gained "3|Custom|200a2a,4a1060,8a2090,c04ab0,e89a60,ffe0a0"
                   (the uniform form, ids 1 and 2 untouched, 3 the lowest free)
  bgAnimGradientRef  "" -> "c3"
  bgAnimTheme        18 -> 0
  bgAnimCustomTheme  cleared
  bgAnimThemeMap     unchanged, byte for byte

The panel drew exactly the same pixels. strip sha256
6f317b4fb873994eff3fda9a57531f61b1b1d8e77abf62f1ff832d5ac232a3fc before and
after at 100/100 on both framebuffers, and
9c7301e9ce49d76d2464b62ecb72fef333b4f9364502c0b7cb10d2720b70e54e before and
after at 60/65. 38,400 bytes per capture, 0 differing bytes.

THE OTHER FIVE FIXTURES

Second boot: every gradient field identical, no new library entry.

Leftover custom string on an already migrated device: bgAnimCustomTheme set to
"ff0000,00ff00,0000ff,ffff00,00ffff,ff00ff" with bgAnimTheme 0 and the ref
still c3. After a boot the string was copied in as entry 4 and cleared, and
nothing about the selection moved: ref still c3, theme still 0, and the panel
still drew entry 3. An inactive leftover never became the selection.

Deferred: library filled to the 12-entry cap, bgAnimTheme 18 and a valid custom
string, empty ref. After a boot not one field changed, the panel drew the
legacy custom gradient, and the serial log carried
"W (11662) DefaultUI: custom gradient left where it is: the gradient library is
full". The on-display Animation category showed the Gradient all row as
"Custom (legacy)" and its swatch ran 082d08 to cefbbd, which is that gradient
and not built-in 18.

Unresolved global ref: bgAnimGradientRef "c99" with bgAnimTheme 18 and a valid
custom string. After a boot the ref was preserved, the gradient was copied into
the library as entry 3 without being activated, the legacy pair was retained
because the ref could resolve later, the map was unchanged, and the effective
gradient was the same.

Explicit refs beside the frozen sentinel, on real NVS: with bgAnimTheme 18 and
a valid custom string held throughout, map slot 23 set to "18" drew Cappuccino
and set to "59" drew Steel, and cleared it went back to the custom gradient.
Legacy 18 with an empty or a malformed custom string drew built-in 0, not
built-in 18.

RESTORATION

Every one of the 89 settings keys matches the baseline, checked key by key
before and after a reboot, with the three credential fields excluded because
they were never posted. The board draws Aurora again, the same stops it
reported at the start. It carries the clean HEAD display-loadtest build
v1.9.8-sleep9-658-g6a2e910c, which is a normal bench build and replaces the
dirty one it arrived with.

ONE FINDING

/api/debug/fb still drops its response partway. On a fresh boot it delivers the
whole 460,800 byte step-1 dump in 1.2 s. In one window about two minutes after
the flash, every read failed with an incomplete response at every step, and a
plain /api/debug/anim GET took 2 s in the same window. int_free, int_largest
and dma_free did not move between the healthy and the broken state, which does
not fit the heap explanation in gm-nov3.10's notes; the slow small GET points
at the link instead. A reboot cleared it, and 120 full step-2 reads in the
later batch ran clean. gm-6ivh's fix is real (step 1 delivers whole dumps now)
but something else still stalls the response. Worth its own bead.

title: Validate migration destinations before retiring legacy data
description:
Commit 2fd637eb introduced two destination-selection defects in bg_plan_gradient_migration.

The library validator accepts duplicate IDs. Migration examines every entry for matching semantics, but bg_library_lookup resolves the first entry with an ID. Consider:

```text
bgAnimGradients = 1|Other|000000,ffffff;1|Match|112233,445566,778899
bgAnimCustomTheme = 112233,445566,778899
bgAnimTheme = 18
bgAnimGradientRef =
bgAnimThemeMap =
```

Source tracing BgAnimThemes.cpp:519 shows the planner chooses the second entry's ID, publishes c1 and permits retirement. Lookup at line 328 resolves the first entry, changing the effective gradient. This was established by source inspection, without running the C++ fixture.

A reused destination must resolve to the preserved legacy gradient through the production lookup. Handle ambiguous duplicate IDs without deleting or rewriting existing entries. Deferring with the original settings intact is acceptable.

The allocation search at BgAnimThemes.cpp:553 is limited to IDs 1 through 13. With an empty library and dangling map refs c1 through c13, migration reports no free ID even though ID 14 is valid. Search the accepted range 1 through 99999 while preserving IDs reserved by existing entries and refs.

The serialized-length test at test/test_settings_model/test_settings_model.cpp:1466 also needs correction. Its fixture reaches twelve entries and then pads a name beyond the permitted length, so it does not isolate the append-length limit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] A host regression runs the duplicate-ID fixture through the production planner and store runner. Migration either defers without writes or publishes a destination whose production resolution preserves the legacy colors and uniform interpolation.
- [x] An empty-library fixture with map `c1;c2;c3;c4;c5;c6;c7;c8;c9;c10;c11;c12;c13` successfully allocates an unreserved valid ID, preserves the map and preserves the effective gradient.
- [x] Tests cover existing ID 99999 and confirm allocation never overwrites entries or activates previously dangling refs.
- [x] The length-limit fixture passes bg_library_valid before migration, has fewer than twelve entries, and exceeds BG_GRADIENT_LIB_MAX_LEN only when the destination would be appended. Deferral changes no settings.
- [x] The migration fault and reboot tests pass against the original and larger test tables, preserving staged persistence.
notes:
Done in 72da379f on anims/astra.

The fix. bg_plan_gradient_migration now judges a destination by what its id
resolves to through bg_library_lookup, not by the entry the walk is standing
on. An entry that matches the legacy colours but whose id names a different
entry is passed over, and a fresh id is allocated instead, so no existing
entry is deleted or rewritten. Allocation moved from a 14 slot flag array to
a reserved id list covering 1 to BG_GRADIENT_ID_MAX (99999, new constant in
BgAnim.h, the five digit limit the parser already had), still skipping every
id an entry or a stored ref holds. BgAnim.h now states both rules and warns
that the validator accepts duplicate ids while lookup answers with the first
entry.

Evidence for the criteria, all five met.

1. Duplicate id fixture: test_migrate_never_reuses_an_ambiguous_duplicate_id,
   three cases through boot() (planner plus store runner). Built against HEAD
   before the fix it fails: "Expected '...;2|Custom|112233,445566,778899' Was
   '1|Other|000000,ffffff;1|Match|112233,445566,778899'", that is, the old
   planner reused the unreachable entry, published c1 and retired the legacy
   pair. After the fix the copy goes to id 2, both existing entries are byte
   identical, and what every animation draws is unchanged including the
   uniform flag.
2. Empty library with map c1 to c13: first case of
   test_migrate_allocates_past_the_first_thirteen_ids. Fails against HEAD with
   Deferred (1) where Done (3) was expected, which is the id 13 ceiling. After
   the fix it allocates 14, the map string is unchanged, and all fifteen
   animations resolve to what they resolved to before.
3. Id 99999: second case keeps an entry at 99999 and checks it still resolves
   to its own colours after the append, plus that ids 1 to 13 still do not
   resolve, so no dangling ref started resolving. Third case has a dangling
   c99999 in the global ref and the map: it reserves only itself, the copy
   takes id 1, and because the stored global ref is not this migration's to
   replace the legacy pair stays and the effective gradient does not move.
4. Length fixture rewritten. The old one padded a name past the length
   walkLibrary accepts. Measured with a probe: length 3792, twelve entries,
   bg_library_valid false, planner reason "the stored gradient library is
   malformed", so it never reached the length check. The new one is eleven
   valid entries at exactly 3800 characters, asserts bg_library_valid true and
   the entry count before the boot, and asserts Deferred with zero writes and
   every field unchanged. Caveat worth knowing: entry content alone cannot
   reach the cap. The widest twelve entries the grammar allows (five digit id,
   96 byte name, sixteen positioned stops) are 3347 characters against a 3800
   cap, measured with the same probe, so the fixture pads one gradient with
   the spaces the parser tolerates between stops. That also means the length
   deferral branch cannot be reached by a library the shipped writers produce.
5. The four fault injection and reboot tests now run twice each, against the
   shipped built in table and the longer test table, through a
   underBothThemeTables helper. All pass.

Checks run: pio test -e native_settingsui, 61 of 61 pass (59 before, two new).
pio run -e display-sim and pio run -e display-loadtest both build; loadtest
RAM 33.6%, flash 90.6%. pio run -e display was not run: it does not build in

Not checked: nothing on the device. Another agent held the bench board, so no
