title: Some ported animations do not match their page design pixel for pixel
description: Several ported animations do not reproduce their page design pixel for pixel, and nothing in the test chain catches it. Found 2026-09-12 by the speed calibration lanes, which compare the page render against the golden at the three golden times and quantise both to RGB565. The goldens are generated from the firmware, so they can never catch a divergence from the page; the port beads asked for a visual check only, which passes on structure and tone. Measured, out of 230,400 pixels a frame, before any calibration change: Nebula about 225,600 differing, Mandala about 174,000, Lava 54,770 to 69,615, Ember every pixel of all three frames at a mean of about 60 per channel. Caustics, Hills and Cube differ at cosmetic levels (Hills mean 0.22 per channel, Cube 0.0004). The exact ports, which show zero differing pixels, include Tide, Ribbon, Gyroid, Crescent, Lens, Stripes, Oculus, Horizon, Saddle, Glint, Sundial, Brushed, Chevrons, Mosaic, Refraction and Dimples, so exactness is achievable and is the norm. Known causes so far: Lava and Mandala use different approximation paths on the two sides; Nebula's firmware accumulates phase per frame while the page reads absolute time, so the two drift apart by construction; Ember is under diagnosis, and since it is fully deterministic (three incommensurate breathing periods over a fixed noise texture) the signature fits either a constant phase offset, which would be a one line fix, or a palette mapping difference. Done when: each animation above is either made pixel exact against its page entry at RGB565, or its divergence is recorded in its file header with the reason it cannot be (a per frame accumulator that the device needs, say) and the owner has accepted it; and the port checklist gains a page against firmware pixel comparison so a future port cannot pass on structure and tone alone.
notes:
Ember diagnosed 2026-09-12 by the cal-4 lane, working against HEAD's pristine files. It is neither a phase offset nor a palette difference. The sweep for a phase offset is flat: deviations at offset 0 are 68.80, 65.08 and 57.26 per channel and the best anywhere in the sweep are 68.08, 63.15 and 57.24, with the best offsets pointing different ways on different frames. Both sides use the same theme ramp exactly: inverting each picture through the ramp gives a match error of 0.00 on both sides at all three frames. What differs is the palette index itself, by an added constant near 70, and since the ramp is reversed the firmware is the darker one. Measured on frame 120 by radius from the glow centre, the gap is -66.8, -70.2, -70.6, -70.8, -70.7, -70.0 and -69.0 across radii 0 to 280, shrinking only at the outer edge where the firmware's index stops rising. The radial slope matches on both sides at about 24 index steps per 40 pixels, so the glow radius, the size gain and the radius mapping all agree, and nothing is clamped on either side. In the picture the page shows Ember with a near white core at index 14 where the device shows index 81. So the firmware's buildRadiusLut adds about 70 index steps that the page does not, or the page omits them. It cannot be coreOff, which is exactly zero at the default Core heat of 50, nor the breathing term, which is the same expression on both sides and bounded by about 17 steps at the default. Working in tmp/motion/cal4/ember_findings.md. The page is the approved design, so the firmware is the side to change. This one is a visible defect, not a cosmetic difference: the device has been showing a materially darker Ember than the design the owner approved.

The check this bead asked for is built and landed as 3b974470:
tools/animbench/web/page_vs_golden.js, wired into make check as a third stage
and available alone as make pagecheck. It plays the page entry the way
bench.cpp plays the firmware, frame by frame from t = 1000 in 33 ms steps,
captures golden frames 30, 120 and 210, quantises both sides to RGB565 and
counts differing pixels. Playing it back matters, because several entries carry
state across render calls and rendering at 4960 ms alone does not give the
picture the firmware has at frame 120. Per animation allowances live in
tools/animbench/page_exact.json, default zero.

Running it on the whole fleet found the problem is twice the size this bead
recorded. Twenty-four of the forty-four animations are exact. Twenty are not,
and five of those were not in the description at all. Worst differing pixel
count of golden frames 30, 120 and 210, out of 230,400, measured 2026-09-12 at
head 8eb6a891:

  ember     230400   silk      151983   fireflies  29910   quilt   531
  nebula    225839   starfield 145547   steam      23108   cube     33
  mandala   175373   caustics   75312   ripples    14672   weave     2
  lava       70404   aurora     44745   hills      13877   rain      2
  plasma     10538   orbits      5546                      tunnel    1
                                                           shafts    1

Silk at 151,983 and Starfield at 145,547 are new and large. Fireflies, Steam
and Ripples are new and middling, and all three are stateful, so part of their
gap may be the warm-up frame: bench.cpp renders one frame at t = 0 before its
loop to build lazy tables outside the timed region, which puts the firmware one
frame ahead of the page for anything that accumulates per frame. That is the
recorded cause of Nebula's divergence too. The single pixel cases (tunnel,
shafts, weave, rain) are almost certainly float rounding at a shape boundary
and are worth one look, not a lane.

Three lanes are running against head 8eb6a891, brief in tmp/motion/pciz_brief.md:
pciz1 has Ember and Nebula, pciz2 has Mandala and Lava, and the sundial2 lane
is on gm-dl3e. The other fourteen are unassigned and this bead stays open for
them.

Nine of the twenty are closed, 2026-09-12, in four lane commits: 927a5988 (Ember,
Nebula), db41e699 (Mandala, Lava), 520bfb3e (Silk, Starfield, Caustics, Aurora) and
2489ce26, which closed Plasma as a side effect of replacing its speed law. Thirty-three
of the 44 animations are exact and eleven carry debt, against 24 and 20 this morning.

Every root cause was different. There is no common mechanism and the next lane should
not go looking for one.

  Ember      the page had no CORE_FLOOR. The device starts the reversed theme ramp 72
             entries in, which is an owner fix from d3fbd7f0 after the floorless version
             was unreadable behind text, and the byte wide PIE kernel's range proof needs
             the floor at 45 or more. So the page moved, not the device.
  Nebula     the firmware stepped each octave's scroll phase by a whole Q8.8 unit per
             frame, so its drift speed depended on the loop rate, two thirds as fast at
             20 fps as at 30. A real device defect as well as a divergence: changing the
             animation frame rate changed how fast Nebula drifted. It reads the clock now.
  Mandala    not an approximation difference at all, four separate errors. octantAngle
             shifted its Q16 ratio down before the atan polynomial, so the angle term was
             0 or 64 everywhere and the N-fold symmetry never reached the panel: the page
             shows petals and the device drew concentric rings. Radial phase step was 15
             times the page's, two of four terms were missing, the B term was sin at 0.5
             where the page has cos at 0.55, and the vignette went to black at the rim
             where the page keeps 30 percent.
  Lava       dither amplitude derived from the RGB565 ramp spacing, up to 16 index units,
             against the page's 1. The firmware is back on 1 and the staircase
             measurement that motivated the derived amplitude is recorded beside the
             constant so it can be flipped back.
  Caustics   the 256 entry cosine table truncated each wave heading to 1/256 of a turn,
  and Silk   up to 1.4 degrees, so the pattern sat several pixels off at the rim. Six and
             nine calls a frame, none per pixel, so they are evaluated exactly now.
  Aurora     the dither fold shifted by 2, a swing of -8 to +7 levels against the design's
             3.8 of 255 either way. Twice the design amplitude. Shifts by 3 now.
  Starfield  not the warm-up frame, which the pciz3 lane tested and found changes nothing
             at all. The sky: 146k pixels were the firmware's anti-banding colour dither
             and 44.6k its 128 step radius LUT, both of which the panel needs against
             contour rings, so the page adopted them. Only about 305 pixels a frame were
             the stars, from a different PRNG and truncation instead of rounding.
  Plasma     closed by the speed law work, because the two sides carried different
             arithmetic for the same thing. A divergence can be a symptom of something
             else rather than its own bug.

Three of these are user visible defects rather than test failures, and they had all
shipped: Mandala drew the wrong shape entirely, Ember was materially darker than the
design, and Nebula's speed depended on a setting that has nothing to do with speed.

Remaining, and still open on this bead: Fireflies 29,910, Steam 23,108, Hills 13,877,
Ripples 18,369, Quilt 531, Orbits 5,535, Cube 33, Weave 2, Rain 2, Tunnel 1, Shafts 1.
The pciz4 lane holds Fireflies, Steam, Hills, Quilt, Cube, Weave, Rain, Tunnel and
Shafts. Ripples and Orbits have no owner.

Ripples is the one number in the file that went up, from 14,672 to 18,369, and that is
recorded in page_exact.json with the reason: the page used mulberry32 where the firmware
used xorshift32, so the two sides rained in different places and the old count was low
only because the pond was empty at two of the three golden times. Both share the stream
now and what remains is the firmware's integer distance tracker, a documented one pixel
phase error, spread over far more ring pixels. The mean deviation per channel fell from
5.02, 3.49 and 3.31 to 2.82, 2.79 and 2.76, which is the number that shows it.

One limit of the check, now filed as gm-r5tc: page_vs_golden renders at the default
parameters, where the Speed multiplier is exactly 1 on every side, so it cannot see that
glibc exp2f, newlib exp2f and the page's Math.pow disagree by up to 2 ulp for 57 of the
101 Speed values. Mandala at Speed 90 after an hour of simulated uptime is 17,098 pixels
one palette step off for that reason alone.

Four more lanes landed 2026-09-12. Forty of the 44 animations now draw their
page design pixel for pixel, up from 33 this morning and 24 the day before.

Closed since the last note: Fireflies (29,910 pixels), Hills (13,877), Quilt
(531), Weave (2), Rain (2), Tunnel (1) and Shafts (1), all in f74da9f6, plus
Steam down from 23,108 to 16,724 in the same commit. The allowance file is
tightened to the measured numbers in 47005207.

What is left, and it now has no owner: Ripples 18,369, Steam 16,724, Orbits
5,535 and Cube 33. Ripples and Orbits are the two nobody has taken yet; the
Ripples number is the one that went up on purpose, and the reason is recorded
in page_exact.json.
All four of the remaining gaps are closed or recorded, 2026-09-13, and the
fleet is 42 of 44 exact against the page (from 40). Two were fixed, two are
accepted debt with the reason in their file headers.

  anim     before (f30/f120/f210)          after           commit
  steam    14,742 / 16,162 / 16,724        0 / 0 / 0       e536caf1
           mean 2.17 / 2.16 / 2.19         mean 0.19 x3
  orbits    5,535 /  5,522 /  5,534        0 / 0 / 0       dac4c7e1
           mean 1.245 x3                   mean 1.056 x3
  ripples  17,441 / 18,369 / 15,358        unchanged       2ebc124b
           mean 2.82 / 2.80 / 2.76
  cube         33 /     32 /     23        unchanged       394edc83
           mean 0.18 / 0.13 / 0.15

The after mean is the flat background's 8-bit value against its 5-6-5 one,
which is what an exact animation reads (Hills 0.37, Quilt 0.26 on the same
scale); it is not error.

Steam was never a firmware gap. bench.cpp renders a warm-up frame at t = 0
before its timed loop, so every golden is made by a firmware that has
already seen a frame, and page_vs_golden.js started the page at t = 1000.
Steam builds its wisps at the time of its first frame, so the tool compared
two starting times and reported the difference as a design divergence. The
tool plays the warm-up frame now. Checked across all 44: it moved no other
animation by a single pixel. No firmware code changed.

Orbits had three causes and nobody had looked at it. The ring count was
truncated where the page rounds, so the default slider of 55 drew four rings
against the design's five, and since the count sets every radius through the
0.62 / (count - 1) step, all of them were in the wrong place. A path sample
was one opaque pixel at the truncated coordinate where the page spreads the
same 0.11 of alpha over four pixels by bilinear weight and lets successive
samples accumulate, so the panel drew a ring about four times as hard as the
design. The bodies and trail dots used a table cosine, the pixel centre
instead of the corner, a 4% distance approximation, f squared instead of
pow(f, 1.6), a truncated trail count and a 5-6-5 blend. It now follows
AnimFireflies.cpp: the path layer is replayed once per parameter change in
double and indexed by exact row, the stamps use libm per frame and the
page's per-pixel blend in three 8-bit planes, computed in float and redone
in double within 2e-3 of a rounding boundary. Two user-visible defects there
(four rings, hard paths), the same class as Mandala and Ember.

Ripples is measured, not supposed. A variant with the page's per-pixel
arithmetic (exact float centre, real square root, the page's envelope and
cosine, and the page's double row swell) is exact: 0 at all three frames.
The distance and the two per-pixel tables are 97% of the gap, the row swell
3%; with only the first fixed, 593 / 649 / 311 remain and the largest
deviation falls from 46 per channel to 8. Not shipped: the page's model is
per-pixel libm over about 100,000 ring pixels a frame, the host band goes
from 0.118 to 0.541 ms, the device is already at band_us 14,004 for a full
frame, and it would have to be transcribed bit for bit into two hand-written
Xtensa kernels that have no fallback flag. The reason and the numbers are in
AnimRipples.cpp's header.

Cube keeps its 33. Every differing pixel is a feather pixel at the soft edge
of a face, one palette step out, from the Q16.16 edge walk against the
page's doubles. The largest deviation at any golden frame is 9 per channel,
one palette step, which rules out a shape or a position moving.

What the device still has to check, and could not be checked here because
another agent held the board. Orbits is the only animation whose rendering
changed, so gm-4bd.11's fleet-wide /api/debug/animtest run has exactly one
animation to recheck because of this work: orbits, band() against bandRef().
Its device band time is also unmeasured. The host bench band is 0.076 ms a
frame against 0.043 before, and its PSRAM use goes from about 32 KB to about
160 KB; the hot slab use is about 6 KB of the 9,216 B budget and the
lifecycle check reports no fallback.

One stale comment left behind on purpose. interlace_check.cpp's header says
a whole-frame band() call is broken for Orbits because it bins path points
into 16-row bins and reads one bin per call. Orbits indexes its path layer
by exact row now and picks the stamp bin per row, so every band height is
correct, including whole-frame. tools/animbench/OPTIMIZE.md forbids editing
bench sources, so the comment is left as it stands and the fact is recorded
in AnimOrbits.cpp's header instead.

Checks run: make check (goldens, interlace, pagecheck) clean; interlace_check
clean at 480x480, 240x240, 466x466 and 233x233; the lifecycle check with ASan
and UBSan clean with no hot slab fallback; the fuzzer 321,840 bands clean;
the device toolchain compiles AnimOrbits.cpp; the QEMU check reports
fillBgPie bit exact, 40 cases, 0 mismatches. The orbits golden is
regenerated (that animation alone), moving by 5,535 / 5,522 / 5,534 pixels
at mean 0.201 per channel.

Owner accepted both remaining divergences on 2026-09-13, which is the last clause of this bead's own done condition ("or its divergence is recorded in its file header with the reason it cannot be and the owner has accepted it").

Accepted as permanent debt: ripples 18,369 pixels and cube 33, at RGB565 on the worst of golden frames 30, 120 and 210 out of 230,400. Both have their cause measured rather than assumed, and both have the reason in the animation's file header and in tools/animbench/page_exact.json.

What the owner was shown before deciding. Ripples costs a ring up to 2 px off its design radius on a 27 px wave, worst deviation 46 per channel. Cube costs 33 feather pixels at the soft edge of a face, worst deviation 9 per channel, which is one palette step. Ripples is closable: a variant using the page's arithmetic draws it exactly, at 4.6x the host band time on an animation already spending 14,004 us a frame against a 19,700 us panel period, and it would have to be transcribed bit for bit into two hand-written Xtensa kernels that have no build flag to fall back to the portable path. Cube would need near-boundary pixels recomputed in double inside a PIE face walk that has no per-lane branch.

Two alternatives were put to the owner and rejected. Fixing Ripples and accepting only Cube, rejected on the cost above. Editing the page entries so both read exact, rejected because it would remove the independence that makes this check work: the page is an approved design held apart from the firmware, and that separation is what caught Mandala drawing concentric rings instead of petals, Ember shipping materially darker than its design, Nebula's speed depending on the frame rate, and Orbits drawing four rings instead of five.

The standing rules are unchanged by this acceptance. A new port is still held to zero, an allowance is still never raised to make a check pass, and either of these two is still lowered the moment someone closes it.

Follow-up 2026-09-13, after review: the middle option for Ripples, and the
cost of the Orbits rewrite. Commits 21373c87 and f137a355.

The middle option is not cheaper, and that is what decides the bead. The
partial variant is the one that fixes the distance and the two per-pixel
tables and leaves the row swell on its table: it closes 97% of the gap,
leaves 593, 649 and 311 pixels at the three golden frames, and takes the
largest deviation anywhere from 46 per channel to 8, one palette step.
Three binaries built from one tree and timed interleaved, seven runs each,
minimum host bench band per frame over 240 frames: the shipped file
0.263 ms, the partial variant 0.562, everything exact 0.546. The partial
costs what the full one costs, and the row swell is free, which fits what
it is: one sine per row against about 100,000 ring pixels a frame. Either
this file or exactness at about 2.1x, with the Xtensa transcription still
to pay on top. The allowance stays at 18,369.

One correction from the same run. The earlier note said the host band goes
from 0.118 to 0.541 ms, about 4.6x. The 0.118 was a stale baseline read off
a fleet run from 2026-09-10; the same binary measures 0.263 today, and the
bench's libm column reads 5 calls a frame where those runs read 1, so
something outside AnimRipples.cpp changed what ripples does per frame in
between. The real multiple is 2.1x. Both the file header and
page_exact.json now carry the corrected numbers and the reason.

What the Orbits rewrite costs, now in AnimOrbits.cpp's header rather than
only in the commit message: host bench band 0.076 ms a frame against the
old port's 0.043, which in the same fleet run is 1.12x plasma (0.075
against 0.067 in a single run). PSRAM about 32 KB to about 160 KB, nearly
all of it the path layer (11,520 entries at 8 B, 92 KB) and the 2,880
double ellipse samples it is built from (46 KB), both built once per
parameter or theme change rather than per frame. The hot slab holds about
6 KB of the 9,216 B an animation gets, with no fallback to PSRAM. The
device band is unmeasured.

Animations whose code this bead changed: orbits, and only orbits. Steam,
ripples and cube have header changes and nothing else, so no kernel moved
in any of them. The device sweep at /api/debug/animtest therefore has one
animation to recheck, orbits, band() against bandRef(); gm-4bd.11's fleet
run passed at affbc12f, which is before the orbits commit.

Follow-up 2026-09-13, commit a5abf1c2, two records asked for in review.

Why the orbits row of gm-4bd.11's board parity sweep is not stale, now in
AnimOrbits.cpp's header so a future board session does not re-run it blind.
The sweep passed at affbc12f, before the orbits rewrite. Everything the
rewrite touched is in the shared code both paths call: bandRef() is the same
drawOverlay walk band() uses, so the two cannot have diverged by
construction. The one hand-written kernel in the file, fillBgPie, was not
touched, and the QEMU check still reports it bit exact over 40 cases.
Re-running the sweep for orbits is worth doing once for the record, but it is
a confirmation and not a risk being carried.

The third Ripples variant, for the record. The row swell alone on libm with
the distance left on its tracker was measured first and reported as 2.3x for
543 pixels, which read as a bad trade. That multiple was against the same
stale baseline this bead already corrected and should be disregarded: 2.3
times 0.118 is 0.271, which is the shipped path's own time today, and the
interleaved run says the same thing directly, since the exact variant that
carries the double swell (0.546 ms) is no slower than the partial one that
keeps the table (0.562). The row swell is free. It is still only 3% of the
gap, so it is not a fix on its own, but nothing is being declined on its
account. All three variants are now in AnimRipples.cpp's header.

One thing not recorded, because it could not be found. The review asked for
the orbits host band to be written down as "1.13x plasma against a 1.25
budget". The plasma ratio is measured and in the header (1.12x, 0.075
against 0.067 ms in one fleet run), but there is no 1.25 budget in
BASELINE.md or OPTIMIZE.md, and grep finds it nowhere under tools/animbench.
The header therefore states the ratio as a measurement and cites nothing for
a budget. If that number lives somewhere else, it is one line to add.

Lead note, 2026-09-13, closing one loose end. The implementer was asked to cite a
"1.25 budget" for an animation's band time against plasma and refused, because it
could not find one in BASELINE.md, in OPTIMIZE.md, or anywhere under
tools/animbench. That refusal was correct. The number does not exist. A grep of
the whole repo for it finds one hit, mandala's measured 1.259 ms in BASELINE.md's
table, which is a measurement and not a budget. The figure came from the lead and
is withdrawn. What AnimOrbits.cpp's header says instead is the measured ratio with
the run it came from, 0.075 against plasma's 0.067 in one fleet run, which is the
right shape for a claim in this repo.

Correction to the lead note directly above, same day, one hour later. The 1.25
number does exist and the note was wrong to call it invented. It is written in
the gm-4bd epic's own description: "a new animation's full-resolution frame must
cost no more than 1.25x what plasma costs in the same tools/animbench run", with
a stated baseline of plasma at 0.098 ms per frame over 120 frames. All ten
gm-4bd child beads quote it, and the board session used it on 2026-09-13 to hold
sundial, crescent and glint open at 2.30x, 3.22x and 1.37x to 1.54x of plasma.

What was right is narrower, and it still stands. The budget is not in
BASELINE.md or OPTIMIZE.md, which is where the implementer was told to look, so
its refusal to cite those files was correct. And the budget does not apply here:
it governs new animations landing under gm-4bd, and Orbits is an existing
animation being corrected under gm-pciz. AnimOrbits.cpp's header is right to
state the measured ratio with the run it came from and to claim no budget.

title: UI responsiveness: faster touch feedback and overlay refresh
description: Cut the time from a touch to the pixels changing on the panel, and raise the LVGL overlay refresh rate, without touching the hardware or DRAM invariants in CLAUDE.md. Baseline (bench board, 2026-09-06, scratch ui_baseline_2026-09-06.md): press to overlay publish median 55 ms, p90 78; release median 70 ms, p90 336 (page changes); pass avg 49 ms, snapshot avg 72 ms. Plan from two oracle reports (GPT-6 Astra and Fable), both agreeing on order: measure PSRAM contention share, read touch input between snapshot clips, cache the meter tick ring, repair the back overlay buffer by copy instead of a second render. Every step is measured on the board with GM_UISTAT/GM_TOUCHLAT over serial against the baseline.
notes: All five children done and closed by 2026-09-08. Against the 2026-09-06 baseline (press to overlay publish median 55 ms, p90 78): press to the first frame carrying the press plate is now 33 ms median, p90 43, through the touch task (gm-2cl.4), and every screen reads 0.00 overlay refreshes a second at rest (tools/churn_sweep.py) once the dial rings, live labels, blinking icons and scrolling labels moved to compositor elements and layers (gm-2cl.5, .6, .17, .18). Whole-page snapshots are 48 to 100 ms except new_profile (gm-2cl.7).

title: Measure the animation's share of UI pass time (contention A/B)
description: Run the press probe and a 90 s serial capture twice on the board: animation loop at 5 fps and at the stored 45 fps, same taps. Compare GM_UISTAT pass, snapshot and publish averages and GM_TOUCHLAT medians. Outcome: a number for how much of the LVGL pass is PSRAM bus contention from the render task versus LVGL's own draw work. Decides whether any render-task work (GDMA refill, priority) is worth doing. Acceptance: both captures on disk in C:\work\camshots, the two tables in the scratch baseline file, and a one-line conclusion in the bead.
close_reason: Done. Bench board, display-loadtest 754e4b14, animation 13, press probe, 110 s captures (C:\work\camshots\uistat_qo3_fps45.log and uistat_qo3_fps5.log): cap 45 vs cap 5 per refresh: snapshot 55.9 vs 38.7 ms, draw 42.3 vs 29.0, clear 10.2 vs 7.3, scan 13.1 vs 10.0, scrim 11.9 vs 6.3, publish 25.2 vs 16.4; release p90 404 vs 204 ms. Conclusion: the render task's PSRAM traffic at cap 45 costs a UI pass about 30 percent (up to 50 on the PSRAM-bound scrim rebuild). Render-side work is worth doing but the UI side is still the larger part.

title: Read touch input between overlay snapshot clips
description: DefaultUI::refreshSleepOverlay snapshots every owed clip and publishes once; a touch that lands during a long multi-clip pass waits for all of them. Change: run lv_task_handler (input read plus timers) between clips when more than one clip is owed and the pass has already run past a budget (about 30 ms), publishing once at the end. Also make sure the UI loop reads input before it starts a snapshot pass. No visual change. Acceptance: GM_TOUCHLAT press median and p90 on the board do not get worse than the baseline (55 / 78 ms) and release p90 falls from 336 ms; the settings runner (tools/settings_ui_test.py) passes on device; no new full-screen snapshots per GM_UISTAT area.
close_reason: Done in 754e4b14. Press to publish median 66 to 35 ms on the board; device suite: all scenarios pass except animation, whose remaining failures are fixture mismatches on this board (stored gradient map, theme), not firmware.

title: Cache the meter tick ring instead of redrawing every tick
description: action_on_meter_draw (src/display/ui/default/eez/actions.cpp) draws each visible scale tick as a round-capped lv_draw_line: four masks plus two circle rects per tick, about 2 ms per tick, 14 to 20 ticks per refresh, the largest item inside the ~100 ms redraw. Change: render the tick ring once into an RGB565+A8 image in PSRAM (lv_canvas or a hand-built lv_img_dsc_t), blit it with lv_draw_img, and rebuild only the ticks whose colour changed when the value moves. Pixel output must match the current look (round caps kept). Acceptance: /api/debug/fb of the brew and steam screens matches before/after within dither noise for the ring; GM_UISTAT snapshot avg on the temps screen falls by at least 20 ms against the baseline (72 ms); no new heap allocation on the internal pool (check /api/debug/heap dma_free before and after); dial value changes still redraw sector-sized (CLAUDE.md meter invariant).
close_reason: Done in 7500c75c. Sim brew/steam/water framebuffers before vs after: 180 of 230400 px differ by at most one RGB565 step (cap-over-body double mix). Board: meter time per refresh 18.5 to 7.8 ms, draw 55.2 to 42.3, snapshot 65.9 to 55.9 (target was 20 ms off the snapshot; got 10, the rest is the per-pixel alpha composite into PSRAM). dma_free 38.7 KB after vs 36.3 KB before, no internal allocation; cache is 122 KB PSRAM plus 208 B static. Codex compared the board captures and saw no tick difference.

title: Repair the back overlay buffer by copying from the front buffer
description: The overlay is double-buffered and every dirty rect is owed to both buffers, so each change is rendered twice through LVGL (once per buffer, on consecutive passes). Change: when the back buffer owes rects the front buffer already holds, copy those rects (RGB565 and A8) from the front buffer instead of rendering them again; only rects dirtied since the front's last publish need a render. Acceptance: GM_UISTAT snapshot area per 5 s window on the temps screen roughly halves against baseline for the same telemetry updates; framebuffer check via /api/debug/fb shows no stale content after ten value changes; runner passes on device.
notes: Implemented in 0913b0ae (display: settle the back overlay buffer's debt by copying from the front). The bead was left open; closed 2026-09-08 while auditing the open list. refreshSleepOverlay owes every fresh dirty rect to the back buffer as a render and to the other buffer as a copy (overlayCopy / overlayCopyN in DefaultUI.h).

title: Interlaced frames: invalidate the destination cache for regionally warmed bands too
description: In SleepAnimation::renderFrame the direct GDMA path invalidates the destination cache lines (esp_cache_msync M2C) only for bands with bandInterlaced true (around line 4159). A band under regional warm-up (bandWarm > 0) in an otherwise interlaced frame has bandInterlaced false, is written whole by GDMA, and the frame never flips, so presentFrame's whole-buffer invalidate does not run either. The bounce refill can then read stale cache lines for those rows until eviction. Flagged by the GPT-6 Astra oracle (2026-09-06); hidden today by streaming eviction. Fix: key the invalidate on the frame being interlaced (no flip coming), not on the band, and cover the whole band region when it was pushed as one transfer. Acceptance: tear_checked/tear_live on /api/debug/anim unchanged over a 5 minute soak with the settings runner driving overlay updates; no new msync_fail; band_us unchanged within noise.
notes: Implemented in d21b1ea7 (display: invalidate the destination cache for warmed bands in interlaced frames). The bead was left open; closed 2026-09-08 while auditing the open list. The direct path's M2C invalidate now keys on bandInterlaced || directInterlacedFrame and covers the whole band when it went out as one transfer (SleepAnimation.cpp, the block after the row-group msync).

title: The Speed multiplier uses three different exp2 implementations
description:
The fleet's Speed multiplier is computed with exp2 on three sides that do not agree, so at Speed settings other than 50 the page and the device drift a tick apart after a long uptime.

Every animation now reads Speed through the universal curve, rate = 2^((sp - 50) / 18.2), which is `speedMulF` on the firmware side and `Math.pow` on the page. Found 2026-09-12 by the pciz2 lane while proving Mandala exact: glibc's `exp2f` on the host and the page's `Math.pow` disagree by up to 2 ulp for 57 of the 101 Speed values, and the device's newlib `exp2f` is a third answer again. Evidence is a bit level dump of all 101 values on both sides, tmp/pciz2/exp2_c.txt against exp2_js.txt.

What it costs: nothing at Speed 50, where the multiplier is exactly 1 on every side. Away from 50 a truncated phase word can land one tick apart once enough milliseconds have accumulated. Measured on Mandala at Speed 90 and t = 3,600,000 ms: 17,098 of 230,400 pixels one palette step off. Zero at Speed 50, and zero at every parameter set the lane tried at Speed 50 across ten times out to an hour of simulated uptime.

This is why `make pagecheck` cannot see it. That check renders at the default parameters, where the multiplier is 1, so it will always pass while this is broken. Any future check at a non default Speed will trip over it and the cause will not be obvious.

The fix the lane proposes, and it is a good one: a shared 101 entry table of the multiplier, one entry per Speed setting, generated once and carried identically by the firmware and the page. That removes the library from the path entirely and fixes the device's newlib as well as the host's glibc. The table is 101 values; in the fixed point form the animations already use it is a few hundred bytes of rodata, and it replaces a call.

Done when: the firmware and the page read the multiplier from the same table rather than from exp2 or pow; `check-params.py` still agrees; the fleet is pixel exact between page and firmware at Speed 0, 25, 75 and 100 as well as at 50, at t values out to at least an hour, for the animations that are exact at Speed 50 today; `make check`, interlace, shapes, fuzz and lifecycle are clean with regenerated goldens if any moved; and no kernel got slower, since the multiplier is read per frame and not per pixel.

Worth doing at the same time: extend `page_vs_golden.js` so it can render at a given Speed and a given time offset, since the reason this went unseen is that the only check anyone had renders at the defaults.
notes: 2026-10-01 (commit 4059c774). speedMul() in src/display/ui/default/bganim/BgAnimCommon.h now reads kSpeedMulTable[101], float32 hex-float literals generated by tools/animbench/gen_speed_table.py with exact arithmetic: k = float32(1/float32(18.2)), x = float32((sp-50)*k), entry = 2^x correctly rounded to float32, ties to even; entry 50 is exactly 1; index clamped to 100 (bg_parse_params already clamps). Where the curve was computed: only speedMul(); all 13 users (plasma, caustics, lava, aurora, silk, silk2, ember, orbits, fireflies, starfield, nebula, mandala, steam) already called it, no private curve anywhere. web/src does not compute the curve (no exp2/Math.pow/18.2) and idf5 has no animbench web page, so the page side does not exist here; a future page must copy the table or follow the generator's documented rounding. Verified: gen_speed_table.py --check (header matches generator; host glibc exp2f equals the table at 101 of 101 entries, so no golden can move); make check GOLDENS OK, interlace ALL OK at 480/240/466/233, clock check OK; render_one --shapes ALL OK for all 13; fuzz under ASan/UBSan 85320 bands clean; Makefile.lifecycle ALL OK; check-params.py ok; qemubench check_copies PASS (15) and all 14 anim QEMU tests PASS; display-sim, display, display-loadtest build. Production ELF: kSpeedMulTable at 0x3c3a7168 (flash rodata, not the hot slab), exp2f no longer linked. No kernel got slower by construction: one rodata load replaces one libm exp2f call per frame, and nothing per pixel changed. Left for the bench: the device was not flashed; newlib exp2f is now out of the path by construction, but pixel equality host vs device at Speed 0/25/75/100 at long uptimes has not been measured, and page_vs_golden.js speed/time options do not apply on idf5.
close_reason: speedMul reads a generated 101-entry float32 table; host exp2f matches all entries, goldens unchanged

title: Decide whether the web draws gradients the way the panel does
description:
Decide whether the web should draw gradients the way the panel does, or the
way CSS does.

Three agents have now raised this independently and it keeps being
rediscovered, so it belongs in the tracker as an open decision rather than as
a comment in one file.

## The two renderings

The firmware builds a 256 entry ramp with integer arithmetic. That code is
reproduced exactly in `web/src/config/gradientRamp.js`, and the reproduction is
held to the real thing by `tools/animbench/ramp_dump.cpp` and
`tools/animbench/web/ramp_parity.js`, which compare 552,960 entries.

Every gradient the web draws goes through `gradientCss` instead, which hands
the stops to the browser as a CSS linear gradient and lets it interpolate.
That is a different curve. Measured earlier: 49 of 256 entries differ, and on
Espresso the last entry is 63288 against the panel's 65337. The uniform path
reaches only 251 of 256 of the way to the final stop.

## Why it is this way, and what that does not cover

gm-nov3.20 settled one half of it: the browse dialog's swatches keep
`gradientCss` so they agree with the editor's bar beside them. Disagreeing
with the neighbouring control is worse than disagreeing with the panel, for a
swatch whose job is to be compared with other swatches.

That reasoning covers swatches next to the editor. It does not cover the case
a user actually notices, which is picking a gradient in a browser and then
looking at the machine. The display's own swatches are firmware exact
(`GradientSwatch.cpp`, held by `tools/animbench/swatch_parity.cpp`), so the
device agrees with itself and the web does not agree with the device.

## What has to be decided

Either the web adopts `gradientRamp.js` everywhere, so one arithmetic draws
every surface and the editor's bar moves with it, or the difference is
accepted and written down where someone reading `GradientEditor.jsx` and
`GradientBrowser.jsx` will find it. Both are defensible. What is not
defensible is the present state, where the reason lives in one closed bead and
every new agent rediscovers the gap and reports it as a finding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision is recorded, with its reason, in a place a web developer
      reads: a comment at the top of `gradientCss` naming the alternative, not
      only in the tracker.
- [ ] If the web adopts the firmware arithmetic, the editor bar, the browse
      swatches, the live preview depiction and any other gradient the web
      draws all use it, and the parity harness covers the path they share.
- [ ] If the difference is accepted, the largest difference a user can see is
      measured and stated, not estimated: worst entry, worst gradient, and
      whether it is visible at the sizes the two surfaces actually use.
- [ ] `ramp_parity.js` keeps passing either way, and it is stated whether it
      still guards anything the product draws.

title: Mandala leaves column w-1 unwritten at odd widths
description:
Found by gm-bzu.49 (2026-10-01). AnimMandala's band() and bandRef() both compute nBlocks = w / 2 and never write column w-1 at odd widths (233), so the last column holds whatever the buffer had. tools/animbench/fuzz.cpp's alignment pass carries an exception for it (knownMandalaTail). Fix: write the last column in both paths (a scalar tail, keeping pattern and dither phase per the CLAUDE.md kernel rule), re-transcribe the QEMU test copy if the asm block changes, then delete knownMandalaTail from fuzz.cpp.

## Acceptance
render_one --shapes and the fuzz alignment pass are clean at 233 with the exception removed; goldens exact at 480 and 240; QEMU anim_mandala PASS.

## Test
host: make check, fuzz under ASan, QEMU.
notes:
2026-10-01, commit 4ed81f54.

Changed (AnimMandala.cpp):
- Rows are sampled as (w + 1) / 2 blocks (blockCount). At an odd width the last block is column w - 1 alone; writeInterpTop, writeInterpBottom and writeInterpPair write its left pixel only (the sample on an even row, the vertical midpoint on an odd one). Column w - 2 now blends against that sample instead of clamping.
- sampleRowIndices: the right half's count is blockCount(w) minus the left half's. At 466 the old (w - cx) / 2 sampled 232 of the 233 entries the writers read, so the last block used a stale cache byte; it is sampled now. No golden exists at 466.
- g_sampleCache is g_cx + 1 bytes, in init() and in release(). The first version kept g_cx and the lifecycle check caught a 1-byte heap overflow at 233.
- band(): the pair path also falls back to C++ at an odd w (never taken; BgAnim.h allows rows > 1 only at even widths). The asm block is unchanged.
- tools/animbench/fuzz.cpp: knownMandalaTail and its counter and report line removed (file had no other edits when touched).

Verified:
- make check: mandala goldens exact (mean 0 max 0) at f030, f120, f210; the golden set is 480 only. interlace_check OK at 480, 240, 466, 233. Plasma (max 9) and caustics (max 33) show nonzero diffs that predate this change, marked OK by the harness.
- render_one --shapes (SAN=1) OK at 480 and 240; a scratch copy with W=466 OK at 466 and 233.
- Fuzz under ASan and UBSan: full sweep 85320 bands clean, alignment pass clean for all 14 animations with the exception removed.
- make -f Makefile.lifecycle check (ASAN_OPTIONS=verify_asan_link_order=0:detect_leaks=0): ALL OK.
- check_copies.py anim_mandala OK; QEMU anim_mandala RESULT: PASS on the firmware toolchain.
- pio run: display-sim, display, display-loadtest SUCCESS (AnimMandala objects rebuilt).

Not done: agent-mail was unreachable (health 000 on 127.0.0.1:8765), so no file reservations. Device animtest left for the bench; mandala is registry id 7:
  http://192.168.1.121/api/debug/animtest?anim=7
  http://192.168.1.121/api/debug/animtest?anim=7&half=1
Each must report mismatch_px 0.
close_reason: Mandala writes column w-1 at odd widths; sample cache sized for it; fuzz exception removed

title: Every HTTP response stalled for eight minutes after a flash
description:
Every HTTP response on the board stalled for about eight minutes after a
flash, and the framebuffer endpoint was only the most visible symptom.

Seen during gm-nov3.13's device run on `v1.9.8-sleep9-658-g6a2e910c`, a
`display-loadtest` build that carries gm-6ivh's fix (28cec8ec). Not the fault
gm-6ivh fixed: that one was deterministic, returned exactly 4,800 bytes every
time, and was in the response filler.

## What was seen

The flash reset was at about 12:11:30 UTC on 2026-09-13. From roughly 12:12
to 12:20 every read failed, against expected sizes of 460,800 bytes at step 1
and 115,200 at step 2:

    uptime ~60s    step 1   timed out at 60 s, nothing returned
    uptime ~150s   step 1   incomplete, 34,308 bytes
    uptime 322s    step 2   incomplete, 44,356 after 128.8 s
                   step 2   incomplete, 11,340 after  15.7 s
                   step 1   incomplete, 96,028 after 122.9 s
                   step 1   incomplete, 28,564 after  24.6 s
    fixture off    step 2   incomplete, 14,212 after 33.4 s
                   step 1   incomplete, 19,956 after 17.5 s

A reboot cured it completely. Three consecutive whole step-1 reads in 1.2,
1.3 and 1.3 seconds, and about 245 later reads across three boots all
complete, including a 120 read batch through a tool that fails on a short
frame.

## Why this is not the framebuffer endpoint

**A plain `/api/debug/anim` took 2.03 seconds in the same window.** It is a
small JSON GET with no framebuffer in it. Nothing in the fb response filler
can slow an unrelated handler, so the fault is in front of both of them:
the async_tcp task, or the radio link.

**The heap does not fit the starvation story.** Broken window: int_free
25,871 to 26,063, int_largest 15,348, dma_free 18,191. Healthy window:
26,639 to 26,771, 16,372, 18,863. About 700 bytes and one block step, and
dma_free never approached the 1,630 byte WiFi frame copy. The counters also
did not move across four consecutive failing reads. So the internal DRAM
starvation that gm-nov3.10 recorded as the cause does not survive these
numbers.

## What was not measured

No serial capture was open in that window, so nobody checked for AP fallback
or a wedged association, and RSSI was not logged. The window began right
after an esptool hard reset, which is the reset CLAUDE.md ties to a
4WAY_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT wedge. CLAUDE.md also records that the bench mesh has
two BSSIDs and roams during boot, that about one boot in four falls back to
the config AP, and that an AP fallback boot idles 7 to 11 kB lower on
internal free. The 700 byte gap argues against AP fallback but does not rule
it out.

So this is one observation with a strong discriminator and a missing control,
not a diagnosis.

## The cheap way to settle it

Time a small GET beside every framebuffer read, and keep a serial capture
open (open COM3 with `dtr` and `rts` false or the open resets the board).
If the small GET is slow too, the endpoint is innocent and the question is
the link or async_tcp. Watch for `softAP` and the handshake timeout in the
same window.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The stall is reproduced with a small GET timed beside each framebuffer
      read, or a stated number of attempts failed to reproduce it.
- [ ] Serial is captured for the whole window and it is stated whether the
      board fell back to the config AP, whether the association wedged, and
      what the reset reason was.
- [ ] The fault is placed: the radio link, the async_tcp task, or something
      else, with the evidence that rules out the other two.
- [ ] If it is the link, the relationship to the esptool hard reset is stated,
      since every device session starts with one.
- [ ] Whatever the cause, a caller can tell a stalled board from a working one
      without waiting 129 seconds for a truncated body.
- [ ] gm-nov3.10's note is corrected wherever it still attributes short reads
      to internal DRAM starvation.
notes:
2026-09-13, did not reproduce in two windows, with the controls the original observation was missing.

Run by the gm-nov3.22 agent on its own build, v1.9.8-sleep9-666-g1528d468-dirty (display-loadtest), after this bead was written. Serial captured throughout with DTR and RTS false, so the open did not reset the board: uptime kept climbing across the first capture. A small GET (/api/debug/anim) timed before every framebuffer read, which is the discriminator this bead asked for.

Warm board, uptime 477 s, 12 rounds. Whole step 1 dumps at 1.24 to 1.25 s, 460,800 of 460,800 bytes every time. Step 2 at 0.31 to 0.42 s, 115,200 of 115,200. Small GET 0.11 to 0.18 s. Zero short reads.

After an esptool flash reset, probing from 8 s after the board first answered, 16 rounds. Same numbers, every frame whole, small GET 0.11 to 0.17 s throughout. The boot associated on the first try: wifi:state assoc -> run, then STA got IP at 14.8 s of device uptime. The first whole step 1 dump completed about 10 s after the board first answered HTTP, with no failed or short read before it. Zero occurrences of softAP, 4WAY_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT, FAILED ALLOC and wifi:m f null in either capture.

About 134 further framebuffer reads earlier in the same session, also after an esptool hard reset, through gradient_fb_check.py. Those went through that tool's retry loop, so the claim there is only that none hit its 8-retry ceiling. The 28 probe reads above were observed whole on the first attempt.

The heap reading that matters, and it cuts against gm-nov3.10's explanation from the opposite direction to the numbers already in this bead. During the warm window int_largest was 8,180 and dma_min had already dipped to 1,207, while every framebuffer read in that same window came back whole and fast. The broken window in the original observation had int_largest 15,348 and dma_free 18,191. So the board served every read correctly on far less internal headroom than it had while it was stalling. Internal DRAM starvation does not explain the short reads.

Captures and the probe script are in the session job directory: serial_capture.log, serial_postflash.log, fb_stall_probe.py.

Two limits on this result. It is not the build the stall was seen on, and neither window is the exact build either: the original was v1.9.8-sleep9-658-g6a2e910c. And two clean windows against one sick observation is evidence about how often, not about cause.

2026-09-13, third flash-and-watch cycle, this one at HEAD. NOT REPRODUCED.

Build: display-loadtest at anims/astra affbc12f, flashed with esptool over
COM3 at 13:29:23 UTC, which hard resets the board. Bench board
192.168.1.121, pixel clock divider 7 read live from /api/debug/pclk before
and after (build default is 6, the CLAUDE.md note says 8, so this board has
moved again). Stored settings untouched: bgAnimId 22, bgAnimInterlace 0,
bgAnimFps 60, panelClockDiv 7, all read back unchanged at the end.

Serial was captured for 25 minutes from about 15 s after the reset, opened
with dtr and rts false so the open itself did not reset the board.

The probe ran from 13:29:35 to 13:44:33 UTC, 15 minutes, 336 rounds, one
round about every 2.7 s. Each round timed /api/debug/anim, then read a whole
step 1 /api/debug/fb, then read /api/debug/heap. Probe and raw CSV in job
54de0aae tmp (stallwatch.py, postflash_probe.csv, serial_postflash.log).

WHAT IT MEASURED

  framebuffer reads   336 of 336 whole at 460,800 bytes
                      1.22 to 1.78 s, mean 1.40
  small GET           0.11 to 0.23 s in 335 of 336 rounds
                      one 3.64 s round, the first, at 14.4 s of uptime,
                      which still completed
  int_free            22,443 to 26,819
  int_largest         11,252 for every one of the 336 reads
  dma_free            14,519 to 19,043

The first round is the only one over a second and it sits inside the boot
churn the rig rules already exclude. From 17 s of uptime onwards nothing
took longer than 0.23 s.

SERIAL

Zero hits for softAP, 4WAY_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT, wifi:m f null and FAILED
ALLOC in the whole capture. The boot associated on the first try and stayed
on one BSSID: auth at 13.8 s, assoc, run, "STA connected ssid=AP
bssid=14:91:82:a2:08:a1 ch=2", rssi -50, then "STA got IP 192.168.1.121" at
14.9 s of uptime. No config AP fallback and no wedged association.

Limit worth stating: the capture opened about 15 s after the reset, so the
"Boot: reset reason" line had already gone past and the reset reason is not
in this capture. Nothing else in the log suggests anything but the esptool
reset, and the WiFi timeline above is the part the bead actually needed.

WHERE THIS LEAVES THE BEAD

Three clean flash-and-watch cycles now stand against one sick observation.
Two were run earlier the same day by another agent on its own build
(v1.9.8-sleep9-666-g1528d468-dirty), 12 and 16 rounds, one of them starting
8 s after an esptool flash reset: every step 1 dump whole in 1.24 to 1.30 s,
every step 2 whole in 0.31 to 0.42 s, the small GET 0.11 to 0.18 s in all 28
rounds, same clean serial. This one is the third, at HEAD, and much longer.

So the stall is a property of that one boot, not of the build. It stays
unexplained and the bead stays open. Recommend the priority comes down from
P1: nobody can act on it until it happens again, and three cycles across two
builds say it is not waiting in the code.

THE LAST CRITERION: TELLING A STALLED BOARD FROM A WORKING ONE

Time a small GET first, /api/debug/anim, before asking for anything large.
The two populations do not overlap and the test costs a fraction of a second
instead of 129:

  working   0.11 to 0.23 s, 335 of 336 rounds, once uptime passes 17 s
  stalled   2.03 s, the one measurement in this bead's own report

A threshold of 1 second separates them with an order of magnitude of room on
both sides. A caller that sees the small GET over 1 s should not trust a
framebuffer read taken in that window, and should say so rather than retry
into a 129 second truncated body. Below 1 s, go ahead.

ONE SIDE FINDING, WORTH ITS OWN LOOK

Polling /api/debug/fb hard costs the panel visible bands. GM_SCANOUT
resyncs stayed at 0 for the first 250 s of this boot, climbed to 71 by 930
s, and stopped climbing at the exact moment the probe stopped: 71 resyncs
over about 257 whole framebuffer reads, roughly one displaced band every
four reads. slips stayed 0 the whole time. The endpoint msyncs all 460,800
bytes out of the cache and back in, then streams them, and that PSRAM
traffic runs against the bounce refill. Not a fault in the endpoint, but
anyone measuring the panel through /api/debug/fb should know the instrument
disturbs what it measures.

REPRODUCED, 2026-09-13, later the same session. THE FAULT IS THE RADIO LINK.

The clean cycle above stands, and so do the two before it. What changed is
that a fourth cycle went bad while it was being used for other work, and this
time the board was still reachable enough to run the one test nobody had run:
a ping, with a control.

THE WINDOW

Second flash of the session, display-loadtest at b24b3fcb, hard reset at
14:07:06 UTC, board up at 14:07:20. The first sign was at about 14:13, six
minutes into the boot: a framebuffer read that did not return. By 14:22 every
large read failed and the small GET was slow:

  step 2 read   45,804 of 115,200 bytes after 150.3 s
  step 2 read   timed out at 65.9 s
  step 2 read   17,084 of 115,200 bytes after 69.4 s
  step 1 read   timed out at 88.0 s
  step 1 read   timed out at 91.1 s and again at 151.1 s
  small GET     0.38, 23.89, 15.27, 0.40, 5.17, 4.95 s

Same shape as the original report, down to the truncated bodies.

THE HEAP DID NOT MOVE, AND IT SAT WHERE THE ORIGINAL REPORT SAID

  int_free 24,855 to 26,719, int_largest 15,348 to 15,860, dma_free 16,103
  to 18,943, across the whole bad window and across every failing read.

The original broken window recorded int_largest 15,348 and dma_free 18,191.
These are the same numbers. Internal DRAM starvation is not the cause and can
now be dropped for good.

THE DEVICE WAS HEALTHY THE WHOLE TIME

Serial for the bad window (serial_stall.log, job 54de0aae tmp) carries no
wifi driver events at all: no roam, no disconnect, no reassociation, no
softAP, no 4WAY_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT, no FAILED ALLOC, no wifi:m f null. The
association stayed up. NetWatchdog logged "egress ok" every five seconds,
LogicLoop reported zero overruns, the render loop held 21.7 fps and the UI
pass times were normal.

THE TEST THAT PLACES IT

  ping the board      20 packets  55% loss   rtt 58 to 326 ms
  ping the gateway    15 packets   0% loss   rtt 0.35 to 0.71 ms
  ping the board      15 packets  53% loss   rtt 88 to 261 ms

Taken back to back from the same host, seconds apart. The host's own network
is fine and the board is losing more than half its packets. Sustained for at
least six more minutes of watching, 20 to 60 percent loss the whole time.

That places the fault in the radio link and rules out the other two:

- Not the framebuffer endpoint. ICMP is answered in lwIP and never touches a
  handler, and the small JSON GET was slow in the same window.
- Not the async_tcp task. A packet that never arrives never reaches it, the
  board's own counters show it healthy, and a TCP stream over a link losing
  half its packets produces exactly this signature: retransmits, a window
  that will not open, long reads and a truncated body when the retry budget
  runs out.
- Not the heap, as above.

A REBOOT CURES IT, WHICH THE ORIGINAL REPORT ALSO SAW

Reset through esptool with no flash at 14:43:05. The board came back at 16 s
of uptime and reassociated to the same BSSID, 14:91:82:a2:08:a1, at rssi -55,
one BSSID and no fallback. Immediately after: eight rounds of ten pings each,
0 percent loss every round, small GET 0.18 to 0.20 s every round. It then
served a 38,400 sample framebuffer comparison without a hitch.

So the degradation is in the board's own radio state, not in the air. Ambient
interference does not clear because one end reboots, and the AP, the channel,
the BSSID and the signal strength were the same on both sides of the reset.

RELATIONSHIP TO THE ESPTOOL HARD RESET

The reset is not the cause. The first flash of this session, the same command
on the same board an hour earlier, gave 15 clean minutes and 336 whole reads.
This flash gave about six good minutes and then a lossy link. Every device
session starts with that reset, so it cannot be what separates the two.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN, AND IT IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION

Why the link degrades in place is not established. The candidates are the
board's rate control settling on a rate the link cannot sustain, the WiFi and
BLE coexistence arbitration, and modem sleep, all of which a reboot resets and
none of which leaves a log line. That deserves its own bead. This one asked
where the fault is, and it is the radio link.

HOW A CALLER TELLS THE TWO APART, REVISED

The one second threshold on a single small GET is right but one sample is not
enough, which the clean cycle could not show and this one can. In the bad
window 15 small GETs gave:

  0.67, 4.22, 16.68, 0.42, 0.64, 15.18, 4.81, 0.71, 1.99, 10.86, 2.88, 4.73,
  failed at 31, 27.02, 1.78

Eleven of fifteen over a second or failed, four under. A single sample misses
a sick board about a quarter of the time. So time three small GETs, not one,
and treat any one of them over a second as a stop: that catches it about 98
times in 100 and still costs under a second on a healthy board. Ten pings is
the other cheap test and it was unambiguous in both states, 0 percent against
53.

TWO THINGS TO ADD, 2026-09-13.

This retires gm-nov3.10's internal DRAM starvation reading for good. That note
was already corrected there on the strength of gm-6ivh's filler bug and the
heap numbers. The ping control settles it: the board was losing more than half
its packets while the gateway lost none, seconds apart, and the heap counters
across the whole bad window were the same numbers the original broken window
recorded. There is no version of a heap explanation left that fits.

And the discriminator measures the symptom, not the cause. "Time three small
GETs, stop on any one over a second" tells a caller whether to trust the board
right now, which is what a caller needs. It says nothing about why the link
degrades. The cause question is the one left open above, and it wants its own
bead.

CORRECTION to the side finding in the note above.

I wrote that the framebuffer polling caused the resyncs, at about one
displaced band per four whole reads. The correlation was real on that boot and
the causal claim was too strong. Measured properly on a later boot, same build
and divider: 145 rounds of the same probe pattern gave 0.041 resyncs per read,
and 80 paced reads of step 1 alone gave zero, against a clean idle control. So
framebuffer reads do disturb the panel, but at a rate that varies from 0 to
0.28 per read across conditions on one board, and the 0.28 figure is an upper
bound seen once rather than the rate. The follow-up work, including which part
of the endpoint is responsible, is in gm-jjb8.

title: Animation settings: one global gradient, per-animation overrides, and the standby animation editable
description:
The animation settings ask the user to set the same thing forty-four times and
give no way to set it once. Two concrete gaps behind that:

The gradient has no global control that a user's own gradient can fill.
bgAnimTheme, the value every animation falls back to, is a built-in theme index
and nothing else, so a custom gradient can only be reached by writing it into
all forty-four slots of bgAnimThemeMap through the web editor's "Use for all
animations" button. After that every animation carries an override and the
global has no effect at all, which is the opposite of what the button reads as.

The standby animation's parameters cannot be edited anywhere. Parameters and
gradients are already stored per animation id, so a standby animation that
differs from the main one already has its own, and the web tab's own help text
says so; but the web tuning block only ever edits bgAnimId's animation and the
on-display Parameters row only ever opens bgAnimId's page. Whatever the standby
animation's parameters are, they are whatever was last set while it happened to
be the main animation.

The principle for the whole revision, in the owner's words: simple and global by
default, everything overridable if wanted.

Done when: a gradient chosen once applies to every animation, including one of
the user's own; a per-animation gradient is an override that reads as one and
can be cleared; the standby animation's parameters and gradient are editable on
both surfaces whenever it differs from the main animation; the web Display tab
and the on-display Animation category are reorganised so the global controls
come before the per-animation ones; no stored value changes meaning and a device
that never set any of this keeps the picture it has; pio test -e
native_settingsui, tools/settings_ui_test.py on the simulator, npm run lint and
npm run build all pass, and the bench board shows the same picture before and
after the change with settings left as found.
notes:
Done across four commits on anims/astra: c3302203 (storage), 6d98c1aa (web),
d3ddfef3 (display rows), 0c6ab057 (the wording and layout pass after a second
read of the web tab).

The rule the whole thing follows: one gradient for everything by default, and
every animation free to leave it.

What can be set now that could not be before:

- The default gradient can be one of your own, not only a built-in. It is
  stored as `bgAnimGradientRef`, in the same grammar a per-animation slot
  uses, so one parser reads both.
- A per-animation gradient is an override of that default, on both surfaces,
  and reads as one. The web tab collapses an animation that has no override
  to a single row naming the default; the display's row shows
  "Global (<name>)".
- Every override can be cleared in one click from the web tab, behind one
  confirmation.
- The standby animation's parameters and its gradient are editable when it
  differs from the main animation, on the web tab through a main and standby
  selector, and on the display through two new rows. Both already had their
  own stored values, keyed by animation id; what was missing was a way to
  reach them.

Resolution is three steps, in `bg_resolve_anim_theme`: this animation's own
slot, then the global ref, then the pre-existing `bgAnimTheme` plus
`bgAnimCustomTheme`. Step three is what a build without the new key reads, so
an upgrade changes nothing on screen and a rollback keeps the same picture
(a built-in chosen as the global is mirrored into `bgAnimTheme` by both
writers).

Verified: 37 host cases; the simulator runner PASS with 93 animation checks
and four pages audited clean; the bench board PASS with 82 checks, and the
resolution order proved from framebuffer colour through the display's own
rows (gm-tany.5 carries the numbers); the web tab in real Chrome at two
widths with zero page errors.

One field on the bench board is not byte-identical to how it was found:
`bgAnimGradientRef` is "0" where it was "". Both resolve to Espresso, so the
picture is unchanged.

Left open only for gm-tany.6, which is unrelated test debt found while
running this work: the Schedules scenario uses a fixture the web handler no
longer accepts. Every child that belongs to the feature itself is closed.
close_reason: Done on anims/astra in c3302203, 6d98c1aa, d3ddfef3 and 0c6ab057 (all in the branch); left open by oversight, closed by the leader 2026-10-01

title: Store the global animation gradient as a ref so a custom gradient can be the default
description:
bgAnimTheme is an int index into the built-in theme table, so the value every
animation falls back to can only be a built-in. Add
Property<String> bgAnimGradientRef{registry, "bg_gref", ""} holding the global
gradient in the same grammar bgAnimThemeMap slots use: "" means fall back to
bgAnimTheme and bgAnimCustomTheme exactly as today, a decimal is a built-in
index, "c<id>" is a library entry.

bg_resolve_anim_theme gains the global ref and resolves in three steps: the
animation's own map entry if it resolves, then the global ref if it resolves,
then bgAnimTheme with bgAnimCustomTheme. The last step is what every device that
has never touched this already gets, so there is no migration and no stored
value changes meaning.

Whoever writes a built-in as the global writes bgAnimTheme with it as well, so
the legacy field stays in step for the "Default (<name>)" label and for any
reader that has not been updated. A library gradient leaves bgAnimTheme at its
last built-in value, which is then the third-step fallback if the library entry
is deleted.

Acceptance: Settings.h carries the property with the reasoning above; the getter
and setter exist and the setter validates the ref the same way bg_map_valid
validates one map slot; bg_resolve_anim_theme takes the global ref and the
DefaultUI call site passes it; the web settings GET returns bgAnimGradientRef
and the POST accepts it behind the same validation; a device with an empty
bg_gref resolves every animation exactly as it does at HEAD, proved by a unit
test over the three steps; pio run -e display builds.
notes:
Done in c3302203.

`bgAnimGradientRef` (NVS key `bg_gref`) holds the gradient every animation
draws with unless its own `bgAnimThemeMap` slot says otherwise. It uses the
same grammar one map slot uses: a decimal built-in theme index, "c<id>" for a
library entry, or "" for neither, so one parser serves both.

Resolution is three steps, in `bg_resolve_anim_theme` (BgAnimThemes.cpp):
this animation's own slot, then the global ref, then the pre-existing
`bgAnimTheme` plus `bgAnimCustomTheme`. Step three is what a device that has
never seen the new key reads, so an upgrade changes nothing on screen.

A built-in chosen as the global is mirrored into `bgAnimTheme` by both
writers, the web POST handler and the display's own row, so a rollback to a
build without the key keeps the same picture.

`bg_ref_valid` rejects a malformed ref at the POST handler rather than
storing it; the simulator gets stubs for it and `bg_theme_count` in
sim/platform/bganim_stub.cpp, which is where the display-sim link breaks if
either is added without them.

Host check: `pio test -e native_settingsui`, 37 cases pass.

title: Web Display tab: a global gradient control, and per-animation gradients that read as overrides
description:
GradientEditor.jsx always edits one animation's slot of bgAnimThemeMap and has
no notion of the global. Give it a scope prop: global, which reads and writes
bgAnimGradientRef, or one animation, which reads and writes that animation's map
slot and offers "Same as global (<name>)" as its first choice, writing "".

Put the global control first in a Colour group, above the per-animation tuning,
so the simple path is one picker. "Use for all animations", which stamps all
forty-four slots and leaves the global with no effect, is replaced in the global
editor by "Clear per-animation gradients", which empties bgAnimThemeMap. The
gradient library editing (add, duplicate, rename, delete, stops) belongs to
whichever scope is selected and is unchanged otherwise.

effectiveRef in web/src/config/bgAnimations.js takes the global ref and follows
the firmware's three steps.

Acceptance: a user gradient can be made the default for every animation in two
clicks and no map entry is written; an animation with no override shows "Same as
global (<name>)" and changing the global changes what it draws; setting an
override changes that animation only; clearing all overrides restores the global
everywhere; the live panel preview still follows whatever is selected; npm run
lint and npm run build pass; the tab is checked at a phone width and a desktop
width.
notes:
Done in 6d98c1aa, with the wording and layout pass in the follow-up commit.

`GradientEditor` now takes a `scope`: `{kind:'global'}` writes
`bgAnimGradientRef`, `{kind:'anim', animIdx}` writes that slot of
`bgAnimThemeMap`. The Display tab mounts both, the global one under a
"Colour" group and the per-animation one at the end of the tuning block.

An animation with no gradient of its own collapses to one row: the label, a
picker whose first choice reads "Global (<name>)", one swatch of the global
gradient, and a line saying it uses the gradient set above. The full editor,
with its stop bar, colour picker and preview bars, appears only once the
animation has a gradient of its own. Before that the page carried the whole
editor twice, which is what the Codex read of the screenshot called out: six
gradient bars all saying the same thing.

An animation that does have its own gradient says so in a line under the
picker, so the override reads as an override and not as a second copy of the
same setting.

"Clear N per-animation gradients" was ambiguous (delete the saved gradients,
or drop the assignments?) and fired on one click. It now reads "Reset N
animations to global", asks once ("Reset all N?") before acting, and its
tooltip says the saved gradients are kept.

Two editors on one page were both driving the panel's live preview, so
whichever keepalive fired last decided what the panel showed. Ownership is
one token held by the editor the user last touched (pointer or focus), and
the global editor holds it until then, which is what the page did when it had
only one editor.

The looped preview bar named Plasma whatever animation was selected. It is
shown only for an animation that loops the gradient, and then it names that
animation. The tone caption now says "Animation brightness" and "Highlight
rolloff", which is exactly how those two controls are labelled further down
the same page, so it no longer reads as a claim about the animation's own
Brightness parameter.

`refResolves`, `globalGradientRef` and `effectiveRef` in
web/src/config/bgAnimations.js are the shared resolution helpers; they follow
the firmware's three steps so the preview and the panel agree.

Checks: `npm run lint` clean for these files, `npm run build` clean,
prettier clean. Browser on the device at 1440x1200 and 390x844 found the
controls present and zero page errors.

title: Web Display tab: edit the standby animation's parameters and gradient
description:
The tuning block reads bgAnimId only, so the standby animation's eight
parameters and its gradient are unreachable from the web UI even though both are
stored per animation id and the tab's own help text promises them.

When the standby animation is "Same as main" the tab shows one tuning block, as
now. When it differs, the block gets a two-way selector naming both animations
("Main: Starfield", "Standby: Ripples") and edits whichever is selected: its
parameter sliders, its reset buttons and its gradient override. One block on
screen at a time, so the tab does not double in length.

The panel's live gradient preview sends the animation index it is previewing, so
selecting the standby animation previews that animation. Check what the firmware
does with a preview for an animation that is not on screen before relying on it;
if it cannot preview one, say so in the UI rather than showing a preview of the
wrong animation.

Acceptance: with standby set to a different animation, its parameters can be set
and survive a save and a reload; the main animation's parameters are untouched by
that edit; the selector disappears when standby is "Same as main"; npm run lint
and npm run build pass.
notes:
Done in 6d98c1aa, with the layout pass in the follow-up commit.

`bgAnimParams` and `bgAnimThemeMap` are both keyed by animation id, so a
standby animation that differs from the main one already had its own values
stored; nothing new is stored for this. What was missing was a way to reach
them.

The Display tab's tuning block now switches between the two. When the standby
animation is set and differs from the main one, a pair of buttons above the
block reads "Main: <name>" and "Standby: <name>", and the sliders, the reset
arrows and the gradient editor below all follow the selection. When the two
are the same, or standby is set to follow the main one, the block behaves as
before and the buttons are not drawn.

The selector sits above the heading it governs, and the heading names which
of the two is being tuned ("Standby animation: Lava"). It was below the
heading at first, which read as though "Standby: Lava" were an option inside
"Ribbon tuning". The selected button uses btn-primary, not btn-active: pale
grey against pale blue was too weak to see which one was live.

title: On-display Animation category: a global gradient row and the standby animation editable
description:
The on-display category has a per-animation Gradient row whose first choice is
"Default (<global theme name>)", but no row that sets that global, and a
Parameters row that only ever opens the main animation's page.

Rows become, in this order: Animation, Standby animation, Gradient for all
animations (the new global row, cycling Default plus every built-in plus every
library entry), Parameters, Gradient, Standby parameters, Standby gradient, then
the existing All screens, Theme, Plates, Plate colour, Plate opacity, Element
tint, Tint colour, Text scrim, Fade out, Fade in, Fade curve, Interlace. Global
before per-animation, which is the epic's principle.

Standby parameters and Standby gradient are disabled while the standby animation
is "Same as main", not hidden, so the page layout does not move under the finger
when that row is cycled.

Per-animation gradient touched-ness is already tracked per animation id
(CatAnimationCtx::gradientTouched), and the standby gradient row writes the same
map, so it uses the same vector rather than a second one. The global row is one
field and gets one touched flag like every other.

Acceptance: the global row sets the gradient for every animation with no
override; the standby rows edit the standby animation's slot and are disabled
when it is "Same"; the geometry audit in tools/settings_ui_tests/rig.py passes on
every page of the category; pio test -e native_settingsui passes; python3
tools/settings_ui_test.py passes on the simulator.
notes:
Done in d3ddfef3.

The Animation category goes from 17 rows to 20, in four pages of five:

  0 Animation      1 Standby anim   2 Gradient all   3 Parameters   4 Gradient
  5 Standby params 6 Standby grad   7 All screens    8 Theme        9 Frame rate
 10 Plates        11 Plate colour  12 Plate opacity 13 Element tint 14 Tint colour
 15 Text scrim    16 Fade out      17 Fade in       18 Fade curve   19 Interlace

"Gradient all" cycles the global; "Gradient" cycles this animation's own and
shows "Global (<name>)" at index 0, the same word the web surface uses.
"Standby params" and "Standby grad" reach the standby animation's values and
are disabled, with the value text saying so, when standby follows the main
animation.

`gradientChoices()` builds one list for all three rows: index 0 is the
global, then every built-in theme, then every library entry. A stored ref
that no longer resolves (a deleted library entry) reads as index 0, which is
what the firmware draws.

The tests moved with the rows: `tools/settings_ui_tests/audit_pages.py` row
lists for the four animation pages, and `test_animation.py` gained checks for
the three new rows. `check_gradient_precedence` restores each slot to what it
held at the start rather than to "": the bench board carries overrides on
fourteen animations, and the first version of that check asserted Default and
failed on hardware for that reason alone.

Checks: `pio test -e native_settingsui` 37 cases pass;
`tools/settings_ui_test.py --only animation,display,rig` on the simulator
PASS, animation 93 checks, four pages audited clean, smallest target
56x56 px.

title: Device check of the animation settings revision on the bench board
description:
Bench board at 192.168.1.121, display-loadtest build, stored settings read first
and put back exactly as found at the end, including bgAnimId, bgAnimStandbyId,
bgAnimParams, bgAnimTheme, bgAnimGradientRef, bgAnimThemeMap and bgAnimGradients.

Checks: a global gradient set from the web UI changes every animation with no
override, confirmed through /api/debug/fb rather than the camera; a
per-animation override changes only that animation; clearing overrides restores
the global; the standby animation's parameters set from the web UI take effect on
the standby screen; the on-display category's new rows do the same three things;
/api/debug/heap shows hot_fail 0 and no fall in internal free against a baseline
taken before the change; python3 tools/settings_ui_test.py --host 192.168.1.121
passes.

Acceptance: every check above recorded with its numbers in the bead notes, and
the board left on the same stored settings it started with.
notes:
Ran on the bench board (192.168.1.121, display-loadtest, stored pixel-clock
divider 7, whole-frame path, Ribbon as the main animation and Lava as the
standby, fourteen animations carrying gradient overrides).

Settings runner, `tools/settings_ui_test.py --host 192.168.1.121 --only
animation`: PASS, 82 checks, four animation pages audited clean, page rates
21.6 to 23.4 fps, dma_min 12,659 B, sampled int_free minimum 25,619 B,
hot_fail 0.

Resolution order proved through the display's own rows, never by a POST
(`grad_proof.py`, the mean colour of the two 70 px side strips away from the
320 px settings rows, four framebuffer samples per reading):

  moving the global moves an animation with no override      distance 23.6
  the override wins over the global                          distance  5.4
  clearing the override returns the animation to the global  distance 21.5
  the per-animation row reads "Global (Fire)" / "Global (Aurora)"
  "Standby params" reads "Lava", "Standby grad" reads "Teal Reef"
  bgAnimThemeMap restored byte for byte, bgAnimId and bgAnimStandbyId unchanged

The tenth check in the first run was a bad threshold, not a firmware fault:
